IPLA/Geometry.lean.title: Scaled coordinates for the parameter and the particles
IPLA/Geometry.lean.summary:
Fix a particle number \(N\in\mathbb N\) and dimensions \(d_\theta,d_x\in\mathbb N\) (either may be zero, and they need not be equal). The interacting particle Langevin algorithm moves one parameter \(\theta\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\) and \(N\) latent vectors \(x^1,\dots,x^N\in\mathbb R^{d_x}\). This section works in the scaled coordinates \(z=(\theta,z_1,\dots,z_N)\) with \(z_i=x^i/\sqrt N\), that is, in the Euclidean space

\[\mathcal Z=\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times(\mathbb R^{d_x})^N,\qquad \|z\|^2=\|\theta\|^2+\sum_{i=1}^N\|z_i\|^2=\|\theta\|^2+\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\|x^i\|^2 .\]

A parameter–latent pair lies in \(\mathcal J=\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_x}\). Given a pair potential \(U:\mathcal J\to\mathbb R\) (in the application \(U=U_y\), the negative log joint density for fixed data \(y\)), the pair extraction maps \(J_i:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal J\), \(J_iz=(\theta,\sqrt N z_i)\), and the lifted potential \(V_N(z)=\sum_{i=1}^NU(J_iz)\) are defined. The central identity is \(\sum_i\|J_iz\|^2=N\|z\|^2\).

From it we prove: \(\dim\mathcal Z=d_\theta+Nd_x\); if \(U\) is \(m\)-strongly convex then \(V_N\) is \(Nm\)-strongly convex; if \(U\) is differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient then \(\nabla V_N\) is \(NL\)-Lipschitz; the parameter block of \(\nabla V_N\) is the sum of the pair parameter gradients and the \(i\)-th latent block is \(\sqrt N\) times the \(i\)-th pair latent gradient; the projection \(z\mapsto\theta\) does not increase norms; and the Euler step for \(V_N\) with step \(h/N\), rewritten in the physical coordinates \(x^i=\sqrt Nz_i\), is exactly the interacting particle update with step \(h\). These facts are the inputs of the convergence theorem for the unadjusted Langevin algorithm applied to \(V_N\), of the identification of that algorithm with the particle recursion, and of the passage from the full state to the parameter.

steps.title: The coordinate spaces and their dimensions
steps.body:
Definitions. Let \(I=\{1,\dots,d_\theta\}\sqcup(\{1,\dots,N\}\times\{1,\dots,d_x\})\) be the disjoint union of the parameter indices and the pairs (particle, latent index). The state space \(\mathcal Z\) is the space of real functions on \(I\) with the Euclidean inner product \(\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{a\in I}z_aw_a\). We write \(\theta_j=z_{(\theta,j)}\) for the parameter coordinates and \(z_{i,j}\) for coordinate \(j\) of the \(i\)-th scaled latent block \(z_i\in\mathbb R^{d_x}\), so that \(z=(\theta,z_1,\dots,z_N)\) and

\[\|z\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^{d_\theta}\theta_j^2+\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^{d_x}z_{i,j}^2 .\qquad(1)\]

Similarly the pair space \(\mathcal J\) is the Euclidean space of real functions on \(\{1,\dots,d_\theta\}\sqcup\{1,\dots,d_x\}\); a pair is written \((\theta,x)\). For \(i\in\{1,\dots,N\}\) define

  • the block map \(z\mapsto z_i\in\mathbb R^{d_x}\), \((z_i)_j=z_{i,j}\);
  • the pair extraction \(J_i:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal J\) by \((J_iz)_{(\theta,j)}=\theta_j\) and \((J_iz)_{(x,j)}=\sqrt N\,z_{i,j}\), i.e. \(J_iz=(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)\);
  • for a function \(U:\mathcal J\to\mathbb R\), the lifted potential \(V_N:\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R\), \(V_N(z)=\sum_{i=1}^NU(J_iz)\).

Thus \(J_iz\) is the pair formed by the common parameter and the physical latent vector \(x^i=\sqrt Nz_i\) of particle \(i\). The parameter enters every summand of \(V_N\), whereas the block \(z_i\) enters only the \(i\)-th summand.

Claim. For all \(N,d_\theta,d_x\in\mathbb N\), \(\dim\mathcal Z=d_\theta+Nd_x\) and \(\dim\mathcal J=d_\theta+d_x\).

Proof. The space of real functions on a finite set \(I\) has the basis of indicator functions \(e_a\), \(a\in I\), so its dimension is the cardinality \(|I|\). The cardinality of a disjoint union is the sum of the cardinalities and that of a product is the product. Hence \(|I|=d_\theta+N\,d_x\) for \(\mathcal Z\) and \(d_\theta+d_x\) for \(\mathcal J\). \(\square\)

The coordinate formulas \((J_iz)_{(\theta,j)}=\theta_j\) and \((J_iz)_{(x,j)}=\sqrt N z_{i,j}\) hold by definition. When \(N=0\) the space \(\mathcal Z\) is \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\) and \(V_N\) is the empty sum \(0\); when \(d_\theta=0\) or \(d_x=0\) the corresponding blocks are the zero space. None of these cases is excluded.

steps.title: Linearity of the pair extraction and the sum of squared pair norms
steps.body:
Claim. For every \(i\), every \(x,y\in\mathcal Z\) and every \(a\in\mathbb R\),

\[J_i(x+y)=J_ix+J_iy,\qquad J_i(ax)=a\,J_ix,\qquad J_i(x-y)=J_ix-J_iy .\]

Moreover, for every \(z\in\mathcal Z\),

\[\sum_{i=1}^N\|J_iz\|^2=N\,\|z\|^2 .\qquad(2)\]

Proof. Two vectors of \(\mathcal J\) are equal when all their coordinates are equal, so it suffices to compare coordinates. A parameter coordinate of \(J_i(x+y)\) is \(\theta_j(x)+\theta_j(y)\), the sum of the parameter coordinates of \(J_ix\) and \(J_iy\). A latent coordinate is \(\sqrt N(x_{i,j}+y_{i,j})=\sqrt Nx_{i,j}+\sqrt Ny_{i,j}\) by distributivity. The scalar identity follows in the same way from \(\sqrt N(ax_{i,j})=a(\sqrt Nx_{i,j})\), and the difference identity from \(\sqrt N(x_{i,j}-y_{i,j})=\sqrt Nx_{i,j}-\sqrt Ny_{i,j}\). Hence \(J_i\) is linear.

For (2), expand the squared Euclidean norm of \(J_iz\) in coordinates and use \((\sqrt N)^2=N\), which holds because \(N\ge0\):

\[\|J_iz\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^{d_\theta}\theta_j^2+\sum_{j=1}^{d_x}\bigl(\sqrt N z_{i,j}\bigr)^2=\|\theta\|^2+N\sum_{j=1}^{d_x}z_{i,j}^2 .\]

Summing over \(i=1,\dots,N\), the first term does not depend on \(i\) and contributes \(N\|\theta\|^2\), so

\[\sum_{i=1}^N\|J_iz\|^2=N\|\theta\|^2+N\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^{d_x}z_{i,j}^2=N\|z\|^2\]

by (1). For \(N=0\) both sides are \(0\). \(\square\)

Applied to a difference, linearity and (2) give \(\sum_i\|J_ix-J_iy\|^2=N\|x-y\|^2\). In this identity each parameter coordinate is counted once per particle, while the factor \(N\) produced by \(\sqrt N\) in each latent block compensates the single occurrence of that block. This is the reason why the convexity and smoothness constants of \(V_N\) below are exactly \(N\) times those of \(U\).

steps.title: Strong convexity and differentiability of the lifted potential
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(E\) be a real normed space and \(\kappa\in\mathbb R\). A function \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) is \(\kappa\)-strongly convex if for all \(x,y\in E\) and all \(a,b\ge0\) with \(a+b=1\),

\[f(ax+by)\le af(x)+bf(y)-ab\,\frac\kappa2\,\|x-y\|^2 .\]

No sign condition on \(\kappa\) is part of the definition; for \(\kappa>0\) this is the usual notion.

Claim. (a) Let \(m\in\mathbb R\). If \(U:\mathcal J\to\mathbb R\) is \(m\)-strongly convex, then \(V_N\) is \(Nm\)-strongly convex on \(\mathcal Z\). (b) Each \(J_i\) is a continuous linear map. (c) If \(U\) is differentiable, then \(V_N\) is differentiable.

Proof. (a) Fix \(x,y\in\mathcal Z\) and \(a,b\ge0\) with \(a+b=1\). For each \(i\), apply the strong convexity of \(U\) to the points \(J_ix,J_iy\in\mathcal J\):

\[U(aJ_ix+bJ_iy)\le aU(J_ix)+bU(J_iy)-ab\,\frac m2\,\|J_ix-J_iy\|^2 .\qquad(3)\]

By linearity of \(J_i\) (previous step), \(aJ_ix+bJ_iy=J_i(ax+by)\) and \(J_ix-J_iy=J_i(x-y)\). Summing (3) over \(i=1,\dots,N\) (a finite sum of inequalities) gives

\[V_N(ax+by)\le aV_N(x)+bV_N(y)-ab\,\frac m2\sum_{i=1}^N\|J_i(x-y)\|^2 .\]

By (2) applied to \(x-y\), the last sum is \(N\|x-y\|^2\), so

\[V_N(ax+by)\le aV_N(x)+bV_N(y)-ab\,\frac{Nm}2\,\|x-y\|^2,\]

which is \(Nm\)-strong convexity. No differentiability is used in (a), and no sign of \(m\) is required; the case \(N=0\) reads \(0\le0\).

(b) \(J_i\) is linear by the previous step, and every linear map between finite-dimensional normed spaces is continuous.

(c) A continuous linear map is differentiable, with derivative equal to itself at every point. By the chain rule each \(U\circ J_i\) is differentiable, and a finite sum of differentiable functions is differentiable. \(\square\)

In the application \(m>0\), so (a) gives the curvature \(Nm\) of the lifted potential that appears in the contraction factor of the Euler scheme for \(V_N\).

steps.title: The gradient chain rule and the lifted Lipschitz constant
steps.body:
Definitions. If \(f:E o\mathbb R\) is differentiable at \(z\) on a finite-dimensional inner-product space \(E\), its derivative \(Df(z)\) is a linear functional and its gradient \( abla f(z)\in E\) is the unique vector with \(\langle abla f(z),w angle=Df(z)w\) for all \(w\in E\) (Riesz representation). For \(K\ge0\), a map \(g\) between normed spaces is \(K\)-Lipschitz if \(\|g(x)-g(y)\|\le K\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\).

Claim. (a) If \(U\) is differentiable, then for all \(z,w\in\mathcal Z\)

\[\langle abla V_N(z),w angle=\sum_{i=1}^N\langle abla U(J_iz),J_iw angle .\qquad(4)\]

(b) For all \(v,w\in\mathcal Z\), \(\sum_{i=1}^N\|J_iv\|\,\|J_iw\|\le N\|v\|\,\|w\|\).

(c) Let \(L\ge0\). If \(U\) is differentiable and \( abla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then \( abla V_N\) is \(NL\)-Lipschitz.

Proof. (a) By the chain rule, the derivative of \(U\circ J_i\) at \(z\) is \(DU(J_iz)\circ J_i\), because the linear map \(J_i\) is its own derivative. By the sum rule, \(DV_N(z)=\sum_iDU(J_iz)\circ J_i\). Applying both sides to \(w\) and using the definition of the gradient twice,

\[\langle abla V_N(z),w angle=DV_N(z)w=\sum_iDU(J_iz)(J_iw)=\sum_i\langle abla U(J_iz),J_iw angle .\]

(b) Put \(a_i=\|J_iv\|\) and \(b_i=\|J_iw\|\). The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for finite sums and (2) give

\[\Bigl(\sum_ia_ib_i\Bigr)^2\le\Bigl(\sum_ia_i^2\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_ib_i^2\Bigr)= igl(N\|v\|^2 igr) igl(N\|w\|^2 igr)= igl(N\|v\|\|w\| igr)^2 .\]

Since \(T=N\|v\|\|w\|\ge0\), the inequality \(S^2\le T^2\) for \(S=\sum_ia_ib_i\) implies \(S\le|S|\le T\).

(c) Fix \(x,y\in\mathcal Z\) and put \(g= abla V_N(x)- abla V_N(y)\). For every \(w\in\mathcal Z\), (4) at \(x\) and at \(y\), subtracted, and linearity of the inner product in its first argument give

\[ egin{aligned}\langle g,w angle&=\sum_i igl\langle abla U(J_ix)- abla U(J_iy),J_iw igr angle\&\le\sum_i igl\| abla U(J_ix)- abla U(J_iy) igr\|\,\|J_iw\|\&\le\sum_iL\,\|J_i(x-y)\|\,\|J_iw\|\&\le L\,N\,\|x-y\|\,\|w\| .\end{aligned}\qquad(5)\]

The second line is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality \(\langle u,v angle\le\|u\|\|v\|\) in \(\mathcal J\); the third is the Lipschitz bound \(\| abla U(J_ix)- abla U(J_iy)\|\le L\|J_ix-J_iy\|\), multiplied by \(\|J_iw\|\ge0\), together with \(J_ix-J_iy=J_i(x-y)\); the fourth is (b) with \(v=x-y\), multiplied by \(L\ge0\). Now take \(w=g\) in (5): \(\|g\|^2=\langle g,g angle\le NL\|x-y\|\,\|g\|\). If \(\|g\|=0\), then \(\|g\|\le NL\|x-y\|\) because the right side is nonnegative. Otherwise \(\|g\|>0\) and dividing by \(\|g\|\) gives \(\|g\|\le NL\|x-y\|\). In both cases \(\| abla V_N(x)- abla V_N(y)\|\le NL\|x-y\|\). \(\square\)

Testing the gradient difference against an arbitrary direction \(w\), rather than estimating each block of \( abla V_N\) separately, is what keeps the constant equal to \(NL\): a blockwise estimate would bound the parameter block, which collects \(N\) pair gradients, and the latent blocks separately and lose a further factor. Since strong convexity also scales by \(N\), the ratio of the smoothness and convexity constants of \(V_N\) is \(L/m\), independent of \(N\).

steps.title: The two gradient blocks
steps.body:
Write \(e_{( heta,j)}\) and \(e_{(i,j)}\) for the standard basis vectors of \(\mathcal Z\) (parameter coordinate \(j\); coordinate \(j\) of particle \(i\)), and \(f_{( heta,j)}\), \(f_{(x,j)}\) for those of \(\mathcal J\). For \(v\in\mathcal J\) we write \(v_{( heta,j)}=\langle v,f_{( heta,j)} angle\) and \(v_{(x,j)}=\langle v,f_{(x,j)} angle\) for its coordinates, and \( abla_ heta U\), \( abla_xU\) for the two blocks of \( abla U\).

Claim. (a) For all particles \(q,i\) and indices \(j\),

\[J_qe_{( heta,j)}=f_{( heta,j)},\qquad J_qe_{(i,j)}= egin{cases}\sqrt N\,f_{(x,j)}& ext{if }q=i,\0& ext{if }q eq i.\end{cases}\]

(b) If \(U\) is differentiable, then for every \(z\in\mathcal Z\), every parameter index \(j\), every particle \(i\) and every latent index \(j'\),

\[ igl( abla V_N(z) igr)_{( heta,j)}=\sum_{q=1}^N igl( abla U(J_qz) igr)_{( heta,j)},\qquad igl( abla V_N(z) igr)_{(i,j')}=\sqrt N\, igl( abla U(J_iz) igr)_{(x,j')} .\]

Proof. (a) The vector \(e_{( heta,j)}\) has parameter coordinates \(\delta_{jj''}\) and all latent coordinates zero, so \(J_qe_{( heta,j)}\) has the same parameter coordinates and latent coordinates \(\sqrt N\cdot0=0\); this is \(f_{( heta,j)}\). The vector \(e_{(i,j)}\) has zero parameter coordinates and a single nonzero coordinate, equal to \(1\), in block \(i\). If \(q e i\), block \(q\) of \(e_{(i,j)}\) is zero, so \(J_qe_{(i,j)}=0\). If \(q=i\), the latent coordinates of \(J_ie_{(i,j)}\) are \(\sqrt N\delta_{jj''}\), i.e. \(J_ie_{(i,j)}=\sqrt Nf_{(x,j)}\).

(b) A coordinate of a vector is its inner product with the corresponding basis vector. By (4) with \(w=e_{( heta,j)}\) and by (a),

\[ igl( abla V_N(z) igr)_{( heta,j)}=\sum_q igl\langle abla U(J_qz),f_{( heta,j)} igr angle=\sum_q igl( abla U(J_qz) igr)_{( heta,j)} .\]

With \(w=e_{(i,j')}\), all terms with \(q e i\) vanish by (a) and the term \(q=i\) is \(\langle abla U(J_iz),\sqrt Nf_{(x,j')} angle=\sqrt N( abla U(J_iz))_{(x,j')}\). \(\square\)

In the physical coordinates \(J_qz=( heta,x^q)\) the two formulas read

\[ abla_ heta V_N(z)=\sum_{q=1}^N abla_ heta U( heta,x^q),\qquad abla_{z_i}V_N(z)=\sqrt N\, abla_xU( heta,x^i):\]

the common parameter receives the force of every pair, and a latent block receives the force of its own pair, multiplied by the factor \(\sqrt N\) from the substitution \(x^i=\sqrt Nz_i\).

steps.title: The parameter projection does not increase norms
steps.body:
Definition. The parameter projection is \(P_\theta:\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\), \(P_\theta z=\theta\), i.e. \((P_\theta z)_j=\theta_j\). It is linear (each coordinate is a coordinate of \(z\)), hence continuous. The operator norm of a continuous linear map \(A\) is \(\|A\|=\inf\{M\ge0:\|Az\|\le M\|z\|\text{ for all }z\}\).

Claim. For every \(z\in\mathcal Z\), \(\|P_\theta z\|\le\|z\|\). Consequently \(\|P_\theta\|\le1\).

Proof. By (1),

\[\|z\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^{d_\theta}\theta_j^2+\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^{d_x}z_{i,j}^2\ \ge\ \sum_{j=1}^{d_\theta}\theta_j^2=\|P_\theta z\|^2,\]

because the omitted latent sum is a sum of squares and hence nonnegative. For nonnegative reals \(s,t\), \(s^2\le t^2\) implies \(s\le t\); with \(s=\|P_\theta z\|\) and \(t=\|z\|\) this gives the first assertion. It says that \(M=1\) is an admissible constant in the definition of the operator norm, so \(\|P_\theta\|\le1\). \(\square\)

By linearity, \(\|P_\theta z-P_\theta w\|=\|P_\theta(z-w)\|\le\|z-w\|\) for all \(z,w\). Applied to the two components of a coupling of two laws on \(\mathcal Z\), this shows that projecting to the parameter does not increase the quadratic transport cost; it is used to pass from a Wasserstein bound for the full state to a bound on the parameter error.

steps.title: The scaled Euler step in physical coordinates
steps.body:
Definition. For a real number \(h\) (the physical step) and \(z,\xi\in\mathcal Z\) (current state and innovation), the scaled update is

\[T_h(z,\xi)=z-\frac hN\,\nabla V_N(z)+\sqrt{\frac{2h}N}\;\xi .\]

Here the conventions \(h/0=0\) and \(\sqrt a=0\) for \(a<0\) are used, so that the formula is defined for all \(N\in\mathbb N\) and \(h\in\mathbb R\); they only affect the degenerate cases \(N=0\) or \(h<0\). This is the Euler–Maruyama step for the Langevin dynamics with potential \(V_N\) and step \(h/N\), whose noise coefficient is \(\sqrt{2(h/N)}=\sqrt{2h/N}\).

Claim. Assume \(U\) is differentiable. Let \(h\in\mathbb R\), \(z,\xi\in\mathcal Z\) and \(z'=T_h(z,\xi)\).

(a) For every parameter index \(j\),

\[\theta'_j=\theta_j-\frac hN\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl(\nabla U(J_iz)\bigr)_{(\theta,j)}+\sqrt{\frac{2h}N}\;\xi_{(\theta,j)} .\]

(b) If \(N>0\), then for every particle \(i\) and latent index \(j\),

\[\sqrt N\,z'_{i,j}=\sqrt N\,z_{i,j}-h\,\bigl(\nabla U(J_iz)\bigr)_{(x,j)}+\sqrt{2h}\;\xi_{(i,j)} .\]

Proof. (a) Take the parameter coordinate \(j\) of the definition of \(T_h\) and insert the first formula of the previous step for \((\nabla V_N(z))_{(\theta,j)}\).

(b) By the second formula of the previous step, with \(g=(\nabla U(J_iz))_{(x,j)}\),

\[z'_{i,j}=z_{i,j}-\frac hN\sqrt N\,g+\sqrt{\frac{2h}N}\;\xi_{(i,j)} .\]

Multiply by \(\sqrt N\) and distribute. The drift term becomes \(\sqrt N\cdot\frac hN\sqrt N\,g=(\sqrt N)^2\frac hN\,g=N\cdot\frac hN\,g=h\,g\), using \((\sqrt N)^2=N\) and \(N\ne0\). For the noise term, the rule \(\sqrt a\sqrt b=\sqrt{ab}\), valid for \(a\ge0\) and every real \(b\) (with the above convention for negative \(b\)), gives

\[\sqrt N\,\sqrt{\frac{2h}N}=\sqrt{N\cdot\frac{2h}N}=\sqrt{2h},\]

since \(N\cdot\frac{2h}N=2h\) for \(N\ne0\). Substituting both identities gives (b). \(\square\)

Write \(x^i=\sqrt Nz_i\) and \(x'^i=\sqrt Nz'_i\), so that \(J_iz=(\theta,x^i)\). Then (a) and (b) are the interacting particle Langevin updates

\[\theta'=\theta-\frac hN\sum_{i=1}^N\nabla_\theta U(\theta,x^i)+\sqrt{\frac{2h}N}\;\xi_\theta,\qquad x'^i=x^i-h\,\nabla_xU(\theta,x^i)+\sqrt{2h}\;\xi_i,\]

where \(\xi_\theta\) and \(\xi_i\) are the parameter block and the \(i\)-th latent block of \(\xi\). These are identities, not approximations: one Euler step for \(V_N\) at step \(h/N\) in scaled coordinates is exactly one particle step at step \(h\). For a standard Gaussian \(\xi\) and \(h>0\), the parameter noise has variance \(2h/N\) per coordinate and each physical latent noise has variance \(2h\).

IPLA/Model.lean.title: The statistical target, the Gibbs measure and the Gaussian innovations
IPLA/Model.lean.summary:
This section fixes the objects that appear in the convergence theorem for the interacting particle Langevin algorithm. For fixed data \(y\) let \(U=U_y:\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_x}\to\mathbb R\) be the joint potential, in the standard model \(U_y(\theta,x)=-\log p_\theta(x,y)\). The statistical target is a maximizer of the marginal density

\[\ell(\theta)=\int_{\mathbb R^{d_x}}e^{-U(\theta,x)}\,dx\in[0,\infty],\]

which is the marginal likelihood \(p_\theta(y)\) in the standard model, or the unnormalized posterior density when a prior is included in \(U\). The sampling target is the Gibbs measure \(\Pi_N\) on the scaled state space \(\mathcal Z=\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times(\mathbb R^{d_x})^N\) with density proportional to \(e^{-V_N}\), where \(V_N(z)=\sum_iU(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)\) is the lifted potential of the previous section. The algorithm is driven by an initial state and innovations whose scalar coordinates are independent standard Gaussian variables, independent of the initial state; its iterates are defined as square-integrable random vectors and their laws \(\rho_k\) are the measures compared with \(\Pi_N\) in the main theorem.

Only definitions are made here. That \(\Pi_N\) is a probability measure, that a maximizer of \(\ell\) exists and is unique, and that the laws \(\rho_k\) are those of the explicit particle recursion are proved in later sections.

steps.title: The marginal density and its maximizers
steps.body:
Definitions. For \(\theta\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^{d_x}\), \((\theta,x)\) denotes the element of the pair space \(\mathcal J=\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_x}\) with parameter block \(\theta\) and latent block \(x\). Let \(U:\mathcal J\to\mathbb R\) be any function. The marginal density of \(U\) is

\[\ell(\theta)=\int_{\mathbb R^{d_x}}e^{-U(\theta,x)}\,dx\ \in[0,\infty],\]

the integral of a nonnegative function with respect to Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb R^{d_x}\), taken in the extended half-line \([0,\infty]\). (For a function that is not measurable this is the lower integral, the supremum of the integrals of nonnegative simple measurable functions below it; for continuous \(U\) it is the ordinary Lebesgue integral.) No finiteness or positivity of \(\ell\) is assumed. A parameter \(\theta_\star\) is a marginal maximizer if

\[\ell(\theta)\le\ell(\theta_\star)\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta},\]

the comparison taking place in \([0,\infty]\).

Interpretation. If \(U(\theta,x)=-\log p_\theta(x,y)\) for a joint density \(p_\theta(x,y)\) of latent variables and data, then \(\ell(\theta)=\int p_\theta(x,y)\,dx=p_\theta(y)\) is the marginal likelihood and a marginal maximizer is a maximum marginal likelihood estimator. If \(U\) also contains a negative log prior \(-\log p(\theta)\), then \(\ell(\theta)=p(\theta)p_\theta(y)\) is proportional to the posterior density of \(\theta\) and a marginal maximizer is a maximum a posteriori estimator. In both cases the latent variable is integrated out; a marginal maximizer is in general different from the parameter component of a minimizer of \((\theta,x)\mapsto U(\theta,x)\).

The definition does not assert that a marginal maximizer exists. Under the hypotheses of the main theorem (differentiability, joint strong convexity and a Lipschitz gradient of \(U\)) it is shown later that \(0<\ell<\infty\), that \(-\log\ell\) is strongly convex and continuous, and hence that a marginal maximizer exists and is unique.

steps.title: The Gibbs target and the Gaussian innovation hypotheses
steps.body:
The Gibbs target. Let \(V_N(z)=\sum_{i=1}^NU(J_iz)\) be the lifted potential on \(\mathcal Z\), and let

\[Z_N=\int_{\mathcal Z}e^{-V_N(z)}\,dz\in[0,\infty],\qquad\Pi_N(A)=Z_N^{-1}\int_Ae^{-V_N(z)}\,dz\quad(A\subseteq\mathcal Z\text{ Borel}),\]

with Lebesgue measure on \(\mathcal Z\) and the arithmetic of \([0,\infty]\) (in which \(\infty^{-1}=0\) and \(0^{-1}=\infty\)). If \(0<Z_N<\infty\), then \(\Pi_N\) is the probability measure with Lebesgue density \(e^{-V_N}/Z_N\); in physical coordinates this density is proportional to \(\exp(-\sum_iU(\theta,x^i))\), the density (49) of the source paper. The definition itself makes no claim about \(Z_N\); that \(0<Z_N<\infty\) under strong convexity of \(U\) is proved in a later section. All latent blocks enter \(V_N\) through the same parameter, so under \(\Pi_N\) the blocks are in general dependent; no independence of target coordinates is assumed anywhere.

The innovation hypotheses. Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space, let \(Z_0\) be a square-integrable random vector in \(\mathcal Z\) (the initial state) and let \(\xi_0,\xi_1,\dots\) be square-integrable random vectors in \(\mathcal Z\) (the innovations; \(\xi_k\) drives the transition from step \(k\) to step \(k+1\)). Write \(\xi_{k,a}\) for the coordinate \(a\in I\) of \(\xi_k\), where \(I\) is the index set of the parameter and latent coordinates. Recall that the law of a random variable \(X\) is the image measure \(X_\#\mathbb P(A)=\mathbb P(X\in A)\), and that a family \((X_j)_{j\in K}\) is independent if \(\mathbb P(X_{j_1}\in A_1,\dots,X_{j_n}\in A_n)=\prod_r\mathbb P(X_{j_r}\in A_r)\) for all finitely many distinct indices and all measurable sets. The Gaussian innovation hypotheses are:

  1. for every \(k\in\mathbb N\) and \(a\in I\), the real random variable \(\xi_{k,a}\) has the standard normal law \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), with density \((2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}\);
  2. the countable family \((\xi_{k,a})_{(k,a)\in\mathbb N\times I}\) is independent;
  3. \(Z_0\) is independent of the whole innovation sequence \((\xi_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\), regarded as one random element of \(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\) with the product \(\sigma\)-algebra.

Condition 2 makes each \(\xi_k\) a standard Gaussian vector in \(\mathcal Z\) and the vectors \(\xi_0,\xi_1,\dots\) independent; with condition 3, the innovation used at step \(k\) is independent of the initial state and of all earlier innovations, hence of the current iterate. Square integrability alone implies neither the Gaussian law nor independence, which is why both are stated as hypotheses. In particular the parameter block of \(\xi_k\) has \(d_\theta\) coordinates and each latent block has \(d_x\) coordinates, all independent \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). The hypotheses describe given random variables; their existence on a suitable probability space is a separate matter, treated in the construction of the reference process.

steps.title: The laws of the square-integrable particle recursion
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(\mathbb P\) be a probability measure, \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\), \(L\ge0\), and let \(U\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Let \(Z_0\) and \(\xi_0,\xi_1,\dots\) be square-integrable random vectors in \(\mathcal Z\). Put \(h=\gamma/N\) and define square-integrable random vectors \(Z_k\) recursively by

\[Z_{k+1}=Z_k-h\,\nabla V_N(Z_k)+\sqrt{2h}\;\xi_k\qquad(k\ge0),\qquad(1)\]

each identity holding \(\mathbb P\)-almost surely. The law of the \(k\)-th iterate is the probability measure \(\rho_k=(Z_k)_\#\mathbb P\) on \(\mathcal Z\), \(\rho_k(A)=\mathbb P(Z_k\in A)\).

Claim. The recursion (1) defines \(Z_k\) as a square-integrable random vector for every \(k\), and \(\rho_k\) depends only on the almost-sure equivalence class of \(Z_k\).

Proof. By the Lipschitz property of the lifted gradient proved in the previous section, \(g=\nabla V_N\) is \(NL\)-Lipschitz, hence \(\|g(x)\|\le\|g(0)\|+NL\|x\|\) for every \(x\) by the triangle inequality. If \(X\) is square integrable, then \(\|g(X)-g(0)\|\le NL\|X\|\) is square integrable, the constant \(g(0)\) is square integrable because \(\mathbb P\) is finite, and \(g(X)\) is measurable as a continuous function of \(X\); by Minkowski's inequality \(g(X)\in L^2\). If \(X=X'\) almost surely, then \(g(X)=g(X')\) almost surely, so \(g\) acts on equivalence classes. The right side of (1) is then a linear combination of three square-integrable random vectors and is square integrable. Induction on \(k\), with base case the given \(Z_0\), shows that every \(Z_k\) is well defined. Finally, if \(X=X'\) almost surely then \(\mathbb P(X\in A)=\mathbb P(X'\in A)\) for every Borel set \(A\), so the law does not depend on the representative. \(\square\)

Since \(\sqrt{2h}=\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\), (1) is the scaled update \(T_\gamma(Z_k,\xi_k)\) of the previous section, i.e. the interacting particle step with step size \(\gamma\) written in scaled coordinates; that the laws \(\rho_k\) coincide with the laws of the explicit pointwise recursion is proved in the next section. The definition requires no Gaussian or independence hypothesis: these enter only when \(\rho_k\) is identified with the law of the Langevin algorithm.

IPLA/Dynamics.lean.title: The pointwise particle recursion and its square-integrable realization
IPLA/Dynamics.lean.summary:
The iterates of the interacting particle algorithm were defined in the previous section as square-integrable random vectors, that is, as equivalence classes of measurable maps \(\Omega\to\mathcal Z\) modulo equality almost surely. This section relates them to the explicit recursion computed pointwise: given an initial state \(z_0\in\mathcal Z\) and a sequence of innovation vectors \(\xi_0,\xi_1,\dots\in\mathcal Z\), put \(z_{k+1}=T_\gamma(z_k,\xi_k)\), where \(T_\gamma\) is the scaled update of the geometry section. In coordinates this recursion is

\[\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k-\frac\gamma N\sum_{i=1}^N\nabla_\theta U(\theta_k,x_k^i)+\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}N}\,\xi_k^\theta,\qquad x_{k+1}^i=x_k^i-\gamma\nabla_xU(\theta_k,x_k^i)+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\xi_k^i,\]

with \(x_k^i=\sqrt N z_{k,i}\). We prove that the lifted potential is the sum of the pair potentials at the physical coordinates, that the pointwise recursion satisfies these two coordinate formulas, and that, evaluated at the initial state and innovations, it agrees almost surely with the square-integrable recursion at every iteration. Consequently the laws \(\rho_k\) in the convergence theorem are the laws of the explicit particle algorithm.

steps.title: The lifted potential in physical coordinates
steps.body:
Recall that \(P_\theta z=\theta\) is the parameter projection, \(z_i\) the \(i\)-th scaled latent block and \(J_iz\) the \(i\)-th pair extraction.

Claim. For every \(N\in\mathbb N\), every particle \(i\) and every \(z\in\mathcal Z\),

\[J_iz=\bigl(P_\theta z,\ \sqrt N\,z_i\bigr)\qquad\text{and}\qquad V_N(z)=\sum_{i=1}^NU\bigl(P_\theta z,\ \sqrt N\,z_i\bigr).\]

Proof. Two elements of the pair space are equal when all coordinates agree. A parameter coordinate \(j\) of \(J_iz\) is \(\theta_j\), which is coordinate \(j\) of \(P_\theta z\). A latent coordinate \(j\) of \(J_iz\) is \(\sqrt N z_{i,j}\), which is coordinate \(j\) of the vector \(\sqrt N z_i\). This proves the first identity. The second follows by inserting the first into each summand of \(V_N(z)=\sum_iU(J_iz)\). \(\square\)

With \(x^i=\sqrt Nz_i\) the second identity reads \(V_N(z)=\sum_iU(\theta,x^i)\): every evaluation of the potential or of its gradient in the scaled recursion is an evaluation of the original joint potential at the common parameter and at a physical particle.

steps.title: The explicit recursion and its coordinate formulas
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\), \(z_0\in\mathcal Z\) and let \((\xi_k)_{k\ge0}\) be a sequence in \(\mathcal Z\). The pointwise recursion is

\[z_0\ \text{given},\qquad z_{k+1}=T_\gamma(z_k,\xi_k)=z_k-\frac\gamma N\nabla V_N(z_k)+\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}N}\;\xi_k\qquad(k\ge0).\]

Write \(\theta_k=P_\theta z_k\), \(z_{k,i}\) for the \(i\)-th block of \(z_k\) and \(x_k^i=\sqrt Nz_{k,i}\), so that \(J_iz_k=(\theta_k,x_k^i)\) by the previous step.

Claim. Assume \(U\) is differentiable. Then for every \(k\in\mathbb N\):

(a) for every parameter index \(j\),

\[\theta_{k+1,j}=\theta_{k,j}-\frac\gamma N\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl(\nabla U(J_iz_k)\bigr)_{(\theta,j)}+\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}N}\;\xi_{k,(\theta,j)};\]

(b) if \(N>0\), then for every particle \(i\) and latent index \(j\),

\[\sqrt N\,z_{k+1,(i,j)}=\sqrt N\,z_{k,(i,j)}-\gamma\bigl(\nabla U(J_iz_k)\bigr)_{(x,j)}+\sqrt{2\gamma}\;\xi_{k,(i,j)} .\]

Proof. By definition \(z_{k+1}=T_\gamma(z_k,\xi_k)\). Part (a) is the parameter formula of the scaled update, and part (b) is its physical latent formula, both proved in the geometry section, applied with step \(h=\gamma\), state \(z_k\) and innovation \(\xi_k\); part (b) is where \(N>0\) is needed. \(\square\)

In vector notation (a) and (b) are the two displayed formulas of the summary: the parameter moves along the average of the \(N\) pair forces with noise of variance \(2\gamma/N\) per coordinate, and each physical particle performs a Langevin step of size \(\gamma\) in its own pair potential at the current parameter. All forces are evaluated at the state \(z_k\), and both formulas use the coordinates of the same innovation vector \(\xi_k\).

Then for every \(k\in\mathbb N\),

\[Z_k(\omega)=z_k(\omega)\qquad\text{for }\mathbb P\text{-almost every }\omega,\qquad(1)\]

and consequently \(\rho_k=(Z_k)_\#\mathbb P=(z_k)_\#\mathbb P\): the law of the \(k\)-th iterate is the law of the explicit recursion evaluated at the random initial state and innovations.

Proof. We prove (1) by induction on \(k\).

Base case. \(Z_0\) is the given initial state and \(z_0(\omega)=Z_0(\omega)\) by definition, so (1) holds for every \(\omega\).

Inductive step. Assume (1) for \(k\), and let \(E_2\) be the event of probability one on which \(Z_k(\omega)=z_k(\omega)\). The successor \(Z_{k+1}\) is an equivalence class built from \(Z_k\), the drift \(\nabla V_N(Z_k)\) and \(\xi_k\) by linear operations. A representative of a sum, of a scalar multiple, and of the drift agrees almost surely with the corresponding pointwise expression, so there is an event \(E_1\) of probability one on which

\[Z_{k+1}(\omega)=Z_k(\omega)-\frac\gamma N\nabla V_N\bigl(Z_k(\omega)\bigr)+\sqrt{2\cdot\frac\gamma N}\;\xi_k(\omega).\]

The complement of \(E_1\cap E_2\) is the union of two null sets, hence null. For \(\omega\in E_1\cap E_2\) we substitute \(Z_k(\omega)=z_k(\omega)\) and use \(2\cdot\frac\gamma N=\frac{2\gamma}N\):

\[Z_{k+1}(\omega)=z_k(\omega)-\frac\gamma N\nabla V_N\bigl(z_k(\omega)\bigr)+\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}N}\;\xi_k(\omega)=T_\gamma\bigl(z_k(\omega),\xi_k(\omega)\bigr)=z_{k+1}(\omega).\]

This is (1) for \(k+1\). Each step intersects only two events, so no choice over uncountably many indices occurs.

Laws. If two maps \(X,Y:\Omega\to\mathcal Z\) agree outside a null set \(E\), then for every Borel set \(A\) the events \(\{X\in A\}\) and \(\{Y\in A\}\) differ by a subset of \(E\), so \(\mathbb P(X\in A)=\mathbb P(Y\in A)\) and \(X_\#\mathbb P=Y_\#\mathbb P\). Applying this to (1) gives \(\rho_k=(z_k)_\#\mathbb P\). \(\square\)

Together with the coordinate formulas of the previous step, this shows that the measures \(\rho_k\) to which the convergence theorem applies are the laws of the interacting particle algorithm in its usual form, with the noise coefficients \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\) and \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\).

IPLA/AlgorithmLaw.lean.title: The law of the Gaussian particle algorithm depends only on the initial law
IPLA/AlgorithmLaw.lean.summary:
Let \(I\) be the index set of the coordinates of the scaled state space \(\mathcal Z\) and \(K=\mathbb N\times I\) the countable set of pairs (iteration, coordinate). This section shows that the Gaussian innovation hypotheses determine the joint law of the whole innovation sequence: it is the image \(\mathcal G\) of the product measure \(\bigotimes_{(k,a)\in K}\mathcal N(0,1)\) on \(\mathbb R^K\) under the map that groups the scalar coordinates of each iteration into a vector of \(\mathcal Z\). Together with the independence of the initial state, the law \(\rho_k\) of the \(k\)-th iterate is therefore

\[\rho_k=(\Phi_k)_\#\bigl(\mu_0\otimes\mathcal G\bigr),\]

where \(\mu_0\) is the law of the initial state and \(\Phi_k(z_0,(u_n)_n)\) is the \(k\)-th iterate of the deterministic recursion \(z_{n+1}=T_\gamma(z_n,u_n)\). This recursion is identical to the Euler scheme of the unadjusted Langevin algorithm for the lifted potential \(V_N\) with step \(\gamma/N\). In particular two realizations of the algorithm with the same initial law have the same laws \(\rho_k\) at all iterations, even if they are defined on different probability spaces. This is what allows the convergence proof to replace a given realization by a convenient one built on a product space that also carries a Brownian reference process.

steps.title: The canonical Gaussian innovation law
steps.body:
Definitions. Let \(K=\mathbb N\times I\), where the first component of \((k,a)\in K\) is an iteration and the second a coordinate of \(\mathcal Z\) (a parameter coordinate or a pair (particle, latent coordinate)). Equip \(\mathbb R^K\) and \(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\) with their product \(\sigma\)-algebras, generated by the coordinate maps. Define

  • the flat noise law \(\gamma_K=\bigotimes_{(k,a)\in K}\mathcal N(0,1)\), the product probability measure on \(\mathbb R^K\): the unique probability measure under which the coordinates are independent with law \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), i.e. for every finite \(F\subseteq K\) and Borel sets \(A_j\subseteq\mathbb R\), \(\gamma_K\{w:w_j\in A_j\ \forall j\in F\}=\prod_{j\in F}\mathcal N(0,1)(A_j)\);
  • the packing map \(\operatorname{pack}:\mathbb R^K\to\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\), \((\operatorname{pack}w)_k=(w_{(k,a)})_{a\in I}\), which collects the scalar coordinates with time index \(k\) into one vector of \(\mathcal Z\);
  • the path law \(\mathcal G=\operatorname{pack}_\#\gamma_K\) on \(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\).

Claim. The map \(\operatorname{pack}\) is measurable, and \(\gamma_K\) and \(\mathcal G\) are probability measures.

Proof. A map into a product space is measurable if and only if each of its coordinates is measurable. The \(k\)-th coordinate of \(\operatorname{pack}\) takes values in \(\mathcal Z\), whose Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra is the product \(\sigma\)-algebra of its finitely many real coordinates; its coordinate \(a\) is the coordinate projection \(w\mapsto w_{(k,a)}\), which is measurable by definition of the product \(\sigma\)-algebra. Hence each \((\operatorname{pack}w)_k\) is measurable, and so is \(\operatorname{pack}\). A product of probability measures is a probability measure, so \(\gamma_K(\mathbb R^K)=1\). Finally \(\mathcal G(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N})=\gamma_K(\operatorname{pack}^{-1}(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}))=\gamma_K(\mathbb R^K)=1\). \(\square\)

Under \(\mathcal G\), the vectors \(u_0,u_1,\dots\) of a path \((u_k)_k\) are independent standard Gaussian vectors in \(\mathcal Z\): all their coordinates, at all times, are independent \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) variables. The construction uses a single countable family of scalar Gaussians, so it does not presuppose any grouping of the coordinates into independent blocks.

steps.title: The innovation hypotheses determine the path law
steps.body:
Claim. Assume the Gaussian innovation hypotheses for an initial state \(Z_0\) and innovations \(\xi_0,\xi_1,\dots\) on \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\). Then

\[\bigl(\omega\mapsto(\xi_{k,a}(\omega))_{(k,a)\in K}\bigr)_\#\mathbb P=\gamma_K\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bigl(\omega\mapsto(\xi_k(\omega))_{k\in\mathbb N}\bigr)_\#\mathbb P=\mathcal G .\]

Proof. Write \(\Xi(\omega)=(\xi_j(\omega))_{j\in K}\in\mathbb R^K\). Each coordinate \(\xi_j\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) and is in particular almost everywhere measurable. Since \(K\) is countable, \(\Xi\) is then almost everywhere measurable for the product \(\sigma\)-algebra (modify each coordinate on a null set; a countable union of null sets is null). For a finite set \(F\subseteq K\) and Borel sets \(A_j\), mutual independence of the family and the coordinate laws give

\[\mathbb P\bigl(\xi_j\in A_j\ \forall j\in F\bigr)=\prod_{j\in F}\mathbb P(\xi_j\in A_j)=\prod_{j\in F}\mathcal N(0,1)(A_j).\]

Thus the probability measure \(\Xi_\#\mathbb P\) agrees with \(\gamma_K\) on the cylinder sets \(\{w:w_j\in A_j\ \forall j\in F\}\). These sets are closed under finite intersections and generate the product \(\sigma\)-algebra, so the uniqueness theorem for measures (Dynkin's \(\pi\)–\(\lambda\) theorem) gives \(\Xi_\#\mathbb P=\gamma_K\). This is the first identity.

For the second, the path map \(\omega\mapsto(\xi_k(\omega))_k\) equals \(\operatorname{pack}\circ\Xi\), because \((\operatorname{pack}\Xi(\omega))_k\) has coordinates \(\xi_{k,a}(\omega)\), \(a\in I\). For a measurable map \(f\) and an almost everywhere measurable map \(g\), \((f\circ g)_\#\mathbb P=f_\#(g_\#\mathbb P)\). With \(f=\operatorname{pack}\) (measurable by the previous step) and \(g=\Xi\),

\[\bigl((\xi_k)_k\bigr)_\#\mathbb P=\operatorname{pack}_\#\bigl(\Xi_\#\mathbb P\bigr)=\operatorname{pack}_\#\gamma_K=\mathcal G .\qquad\square\]

The conclusion concerns the joint law of the whole sequence, across all times as well as within each vector. Knowing only that each \(\xi_k\) is a standard Gaussian vector would not determine it, because the vectors at different times could be dependent.

steps.title: The particle update is the Langevin update for the lifted potential
steps.body:
Definitions. For a potential \(W\) on \(\mathcal Z\) and a step \(s\in\mathbb R\), the Euler (unadjusted Langevin) update is \(F_{W,s}(z,u)=z-s\nabla W(z)+\sqrt{2s}\,u\). For any map \(F:\mathcal Z\times\mathcal Z\to\mathcal Z\), an initial point \(z_0\) and a sequence \((u_n)_{n\ge0}\), the noise-driven chain is \(y_0=z_0\), \(y_{n+1}=F(y_n,u_n)\).

Claim. (a) For all \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\) and \(z,u\in\mathcal Z\), \(F_{V_N,\gamma/N}(z,u)=T_\gamma(z,u)\). (b) For every \(z_0\), every sequence \((u_n)\) and every \(k\), the noise-driven chain of \(F_{V_N,\gamma/N}\) at time \(k\) equals the pointwise particle recursion \(z_k\) started at \(z_0\) and driven by \((u_n)\).

Proof. (a) Both maps equal \(z-\frac\gamma N\nabla V_N(z)+c\,u\), with \(c=\sqrt{2\cdot\frac\gamma N}\) for the first and \(c=\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}N}\) for the second; the two radicands are equal by associativity of multiplication and division, \(2\cdot\frac\gamma N=\frac{2\gamma}N\).

(b) Induction on \(k\). For \(k=0\) both chains equal \(z_0\). If \(y_k=z_k\), then \(y_{k+1}=F_{V_N,\gamma/N}(y_k,u_k)=T_\gamma(z_k,u_k)=z_{k+1}\) by (a). \(\square\)

The statement is deterministic: no distributional assumption on \(z_0\) or \((u_n)\) is involved.

steps.title: The law of every iterate and its independence of the realization
steps.body:
Definition. For a measurable map \(F:\mathcal Z\times\mathcal Z\to\mathcal Z\), a probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathcal Z\), a probability measure \(Q\) on \(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\), let \(\Phi_k(z_0,(u_n)_n)\) be the noise-driven chain of \(F\) at time \(k\), and define the chain law \(\operatorname{law}_k(F,\mu,Q)=(\Phi_k)_\#(\mu\otimes Q)\), the image of the product measure.

Claim. Let \(\mathbb P\) be a probability measure, \(U\) differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\), and let \(Z_0,\xi_0,\xi_1,\dots\) be square-integrable random vectors satisfying the Gaussian innovation hypotheses. Let \(\mu_0=(Z_0)_\#\mathbb P\). Then for every \(k\),

\[\rho_k=\operatorname{law}_k\bigl(F_{V_N,\gamma/N},\ \mu_0,\ \mathcal G\bigr).\qquad(1)\]

Consequently, if \(Z_0',\xi_0',\xi_1',\dots\) on another probability space \((\Omega',\mathcal F',\mathbb P')\) also satisfy the Gaussian innovation hypotheses and \((Z_0')_\#\mathbb P'=\mu_0\), then the corresponding laws satisfy \(\rho_k'=\rho_k\) for every \(k\).

Proof. By the previous section, \(\rho_k=(z_k)_\#\mathbb P\), where \(z_k(\omega)\) is the pointwise particle recursion started at \(Z_0(\omega)\) and driven by \((\xi_n(\omega))_n\). By the previous step, \(z_k(\omega)=\Phi_k(Z_0(\omega),\xi(\omega))\), where \(\xi(\omega)=(\xi_n(\omega))_n\) and \(\Phi_k\) is built from \(F=F_{V_N,\gamma/N}\).

Measurability. \(\nabla V_N\) is \(NL\)-Lipschitz, hence continuous and Borel measurable, so \((z,u)\mapsto z-\frac\gamma N\nabla V_N(z)+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,u\) is measurable. \(\Phi_0(z_0,u)=z_0\) is measurable, and \(\Phi_{k+1}(z_0,u)=F(\Phi_k(z_0,u),u_k)\) is a composition of measurable maps; by induction every \(\Phi_k\) is measurable on \(\mathcal Z\times\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\).

Joint law. \(Z_0\) and the path \(\xi\) are almost everywhere measurable and independent, so the law of the pair \((Z_0,\xi)\) is the product of the marginal laws: \((Z_0,\xi)_\#\mathbb P=\mu_0\otimes\xi_\#\mathbb P=\mu_0\otimes\mathcal G\), the last equality by the second step of this section.

Conclusion. By the composition rule for image measures,

\[\rho_k=\bigl(\Phi_k\circ(Z_0,\xi)\bigr)_\#\mathbb P=(\Phi_k)_\#\bigl((Z_0,\xi)_\#\mathbb P\bigr)=(\Phi_k)_\#(\mu_0\otimes\mathcal G),\]

which is (1). The right side of (1) depends only on \(U\), \(\gamma\), \(N\) and \(\mu_0\). Applying (1) to both realizations and using \((Z_0')_\#\mathbb P'=\mu_0\) gives \(\rho_k'=\rho_k\). \(\square\)

No reference diffusion, stationarity or coupling enters this argument. Identity (1) is used in two ways: it shows that \(\rho_k\) is the law of the Langevin algorithm for \(V_N\) at step \(\gamma/N\), and it allows the convergence proof to work with a realization on a product probability space that also carries a stationary reference process.

IPLA/Foundations.lean.title: Normalization, moments and the score bound for the lifted Gibbs target
IPLA/Foundations.lean.summary:
Let \(U\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex on the pair space with \(m>0\), and let \(N\ge1\). By the geometry section, the lifted potential \(V_N(z)=\sum_iU(J_iz)\) on \(\mathcal Z\) is differentiable and \(Nm\)-strongly convex, with \(Nm>0\); if \(\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then \(\nabla V_N\) is \(NL\)-Lipschitz. This section applies three general results on Gibbs measures \(\pi_W\propto e^{-W}\) of strongly convex potentials to \(W=V_N\), and obtains:

  • the normalizing constant \(Z_N=\int e^{-V_N}\) satisfies \(0<Z_N<\infty\), so the target \(\Pi_N\) is a probability measure, and \(\int\|z\|^2\,d\Pi_N(z)<\infty\);
  • an initial state whose law is at finite quadratic Wasserstein distance from \(\Pi_N\) is square integrable;
  • the score of the target satisfies \(\int\|\nabla V_N\|^2\,d\Pi_N\le NL\,D\), where \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x=\dim\mathcal Z\).

None of these properties is assumed in the main theorem; they are consequences of the hypotheses on the joint potential. The first justifies the use of \(\Pi_N\) as a target law, the second the representation of the initial state as a square-integrable random vector, and the third is the moment bound on the drift of the stationary reference process in the convergence proof.

steps.title: Normalization and second moment of the target
steps.body:
Claim. (a) For every \(U\), the target \(\Pi_N=Z_N^{-1}e^{-V_N}dz\) is the Gibbs measure \(\pi_W=Z_W^{-1}e^{-W}dz\) of the potential \(W=V_N\), with the same extended-valued normalization. (b) Let \(N\ge1\), \(m>0\), and let \(U\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex. Then \(\Pi_N\) is a probability measure and

\[\int_{\mathcal Z}\|z\|^2\,d\Pi_N(z)<\infty .\]

Proof. (a) Both measures are defined by the same formula, so they are equal.

(b) Put \(W=V_N\) and \(\kappa=Nm\). By the geometry section \(W\) is differentiable and \(\kappa\)-strongly convex, and \(\kappa>0\) because \(N\ge1\) and \(m>0\). We use the general normalization and moment theorems for Gibbs measures and , whose proof runs as follows.

Quadratic lower bound. Applying the definition of \(\kappa\)-strong convexity with the points \(0,z\) and weights \(1-t,t\) for \(t\in(0,1)\) gives \(W(tz)\le(1-t)W(0)+tW(z)-t(1-t)\frac\kappa2\|z\|^2\). Subtract \(W(0)\), divide by \(t>0\) and let \(t\to0^+\); differentiability of \(W\) at \(0\) gives

\[W(z)\ge W(0)+\langle\nabla W(0),z\rangle+\frac\kappa2\|z\|^2 .\]

By Cauchy–Schwarz \(\langle\nabla W(0),z\rangle\ge-\|\nabla W(0)\|\,\|z\|\), and Young's inequality \(ab\le\frac\kappa4a^2+\frac1\kappa b^2\) with \(a=\|z\|\), \(b=\|\nabla W(0)\|\) gives \(\|\nabla W(0)\|\|z\|\le\frac\kappa4\|z\|^2+\frac{\|\nabla W(0)\|^2}\kappa\). Hence

\[W(z)\ge W(0)-\frac{\|\nabla W(0)\|^2}\kappa+\frac\kappa4\|z\|^2\qquad\text{and}\qquad e^{-W(z)}\le C\,e^{-\frac\kappa4\|z\|^2},\quad C=e^{\|\nabla W(0)\|^2/\kappa-W(0)} .\]

Finiteness. The Gaussian function \(e^{-\frac\kappa4\|z\|^2}\) and the function \(\|z\|^2e^{-\frac\kappa4\|z\|^2}\) are Lebesgue integrable on the finite-dimensional space \(\mathcal Z\). By comparison, \(Z_W=\int e^{-W}<\infty\) and \(\int\|z\|^2e^{-W(z)}\,dz<\infty\); \(W\) is continuous, so these integrands are measurable.

Positivity. \(e^{-W}>0\) everywhere and Lebesgue measure of \(\mathcal Z\) is positive, so \(Z_W>0\).

Conclusion. Since \(0<Z_W<\infty\), \(\pi_W(\mathcal Z)=Z_W^{-1}\int e^{-W}=Z_W^{-1}Z_W=1\), and \(\int\|z\|^2d\pi_W=Z_W^{-1}\int\|z\|^2e^{-W(z)}dz<\infty\). By (a), these statements hold for \(\Pi_N\). \(\square\)

The hypothesis \(N\ge1\) is needed: for \(N=0\) the lifted potential is \(0\) on \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\), and \(Z_N=\infty\) as soon as \(d_\theta\ge1\). Lipschitz continuity of \(\nabla U\) is not used here.

\[W_2(\mu,\nu)=\inf\Bigl\{\Bigl(\int\|x-y\|^2\,dc(x,y)\Bigr)^{1/2}:\ c\text{ a coupling of }\mu\text{ and }\nu\Bigr\}\in[0,\infty].\]

\[\|x\|^2\le\bigl(\|x-y\|+\|y\|\bigr)^2\le2\|x-y\|^2+2\|y\|^2 .\]

\[\int\|x\|^2\,dc(x,y)\le2\int\|x-y\|^2\,dc+2\int\|y\|^2\,d\Pi_N(y)<\infty,\]

IPLA/Scaling.lean.summary:
The interacting particle algorithm with step \(\gamma\) is the unadjusted Langevin algorithm for the lifted potential \(V_N\) on \(\mathcal Z\) with step \(h=\gamma/N\), and \(V_N\) has convexity constant \(m_N=Nm\), gradient Lipschitz constant \(L_N=NL\) and dimension \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\). All three are identities, so no constant is lost. They are used in the proof of the main theorem. steps.title: The step condition and the discretization term in particle variables
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(N\ge1\) and \(m,L,\gamma\in\mathbb R\), and use the convention \(a/0=0\).

(a) \(\displaystyle\frac\gamma N\le\frac2{Nm+NL}\iff\gamma\le\frac2{m+L}\).

(b) If moreover \(d_\theta,d_x\in\mathbb N\) and \(\gamma\ge0\), then

\[\frac{33}{20}\cdot\frac{NL}{Nm}\cdot\sqrt{\frac\gamma N\,(d_\theta+Nd_x)}=\frac{33}{20}\cdot\frac Lm\cdot\sqrt{d_x+\frac{d_\theta}N}\cdot\sqrt\gamma .\]

Proof. (a) By distributivity \(Nm+NL=N(m+L)\), so \(\frac2{Nm+NL}=\frac2{(m+L)N}=\frac1N\cdot\frac2{m+L}\); this holds also when \(m+L=0\), both sides then being \(0\). The left inequality therefore reads \(\frac\gamma N\le\frac1N\cdot\frac2{m+L}\). Since \(N>0\), multiplying or dividing an inequality by \(N\) preserves it, so this is equivalent to \(\gamma\le\frac2{m+L}\).

(b) Since \(N\ne0\), the common factor cancels: \(\frac{NL}{Nm}=\frac Lm\) (both sides are \(0\) if \(m=0\)). Next,

\[\frac\gamma N\,(d_\theta+Nd_x)=\gamma\Bigl(\frac{d_\theta}N+d_x\Bigr)=\Bigl(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}N\Bigr)\gamma .\]

The factor \(a=d_x+d_\theta/N\) is nonnegative, and for \(a\ge0\) and \(b\ge0\) one has \(\sqrt{ab}=\sqrt a\sqrt b\). Hence \(\sqrt{\frac\gamma N(d_\theta+Nd_x)}=\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\,\sqrt\gamma\), and multiplying by \(\frac{33}{20}\frac Lm\) gives (b). \(\square\)

In (b) the hypothesis \(\gamma\ge0\) is not needed if the square root of a negative number is read as \(0\): the rule \(\sqrt{ab}=\sqrt a\sqrt b\) only requires \(a\ge0\) under that convention. In the lifted notation, (a) says that the step condition for \(V_N\) at step \(h=\gamma/N\) is the step condition \(\gamma\le2/(m+L)\) of the particle algorithm, independently of \(N\); and (b) says \(\frac{L_N}{m_N}\sqrt{hD}=\frac Lm\sqrt{(d_x+d_\theta/N)\gamma}\). In the discretization term the latent dimension appears with coefficient one and the parameter dimension is divided by \(N\): at a fixed step, increasing the number of particles reduces only the parameter contribution.

  • \(\rho_k=K_{\gamma/N}^{\,k}\mu_0\), where \(\mu_0\) is the initial law: the particle recursion is the Langevin Markov chain for \(V_N\) at step \(\gamma/N\).

Let \((S,\mathcal S,Q)\) be a probability space carrying real processes \((B_a(t))_{t\ge0}\), \(a\in I\), each pre-Brownian: its finite-dimensional distributions are those of a standard Brownian motion (centered Gaussian with \(\operatorname{Cov}(B_a(s),B_a(t))=\min(s,t)\)); path continuity is not required. Let \(h>0\) and assume that the grid paths \(\bigl(B_a(nh)\bigr)_{n\in\mathbb N}\), \(a\in I\), are independent random elements of \(\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\). On \(\tilde\Omega=(\mathcal Z\times\mathcal Z)\times S\) with \(\tilde{\mathbb P}=c\otimes Q\) define, for \(\tilde\omega=((x,y),s)\),

\[X_0(\tilde\omega)=x,\qquad\xi_{n,a}(\tilde\omega)=\frac{B_a((n+1)h)(s)-B_a(nh)(s)}{\sqrt h}\quad(n\in\mathbb N,\ a\in I).\]

Claim. \(\tilde{\mathbb P}\) is a probability measure; \(X_0\) is square integrable with law \(\mu\); each \(\xi_n=(\xi_{n,a})_{a\in I}\) is square integrable; and \(X_0,\xi_0,\xi_1,\dots\) satisfy the Gaussian innovation hypotheses under \(\tilde{\mathbb P}\).

Proof. Probability. The total mass of a coupling equals that of its first marginal, so \(c(\mathcal Z\times\mathcal Z)=\mu(\mathcal Z)=1\); with \(Q(S)=1\), the product measure has total mass \(1\).

Initial state. The law of \(X_0\) under \(\tilde{\mathbb P}\) is the first marginal of \(c\), namely \(\mu\). As in the section on foundations, \(\|x\|^2\le2\|x-y\|^2+2\|y\|^2\) and integration against \(c\) give \(\int\|X_0\|^2d\tilde{\mathbb P}\le2\int\|x-y\|^2dc+2\int\|y\|^2d\pi<\infty\).

Coordinate laws. For a pre-Brownian process, \(B_a((n+1)h)-B_a(nh)\) is centered Gaussian with variance \((n+1)h-2nh+nh=h\), so \(\xi_{n,a}\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) under \(Q\), and in particular finite second moment. Since \(\xi_{n,a}\) depends only on \(s\) and the image of \(c\otimes Q\) under \(\tilde\omega\mapsto s\) is \(Q\), the law of \(\xi_{n,a}\) under \(\tilde{\mathbb P}\) is also \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). This is condition 1, and it gives square integrability of each \(\xi_n\).

Mutual independence. For fixed \(a\), the increments of a pre-Brownian process over the disjoint intervals \([nh,(n+1)h]\), \(n\in\mathbb N\), are independent (a centered Gaussian vector with diagonal covariance, since \(\operatorname{Cov}\) of increments over disjoint intervals vanishes). The increments of coordinate \(a\) are functions of the grid path \((B_a(nh))_n\), and these grid paths are independent over \(a\). For finitely many distinct pairs \((n,a)\) and Borel sets \(A_{n,a}\), first factor over \(a\) by independence of the grid paths and then over \(n\) by independence of increments; this shows that the whole family \((\xi_{n,a})\) is independent under \(Q\), hence under \(\tilde{\mathbb P}\). This is condition 2.

Independence of the initial state. \(X_0\) is a function of the first factor \((x,y)\) and the path \((\xi_n)_n\) a function of the second factor \(s\). Under a product measure, functions of different factors are independent: \(\tilde{\mathbb P}(X_0\in A,\ (\xi_n)_n\in C)=c(A\times\mathcal Z)\,Q(\{s:(\xi_n(s))_n\in C\})\). This is condition 3. \(\square\)

By the previous step (with \(\mu=\mu_0\)), the initial state \(X_0\) and the increments \(\xi_n\) on \((\tilde\Omega,c\otimes Q)\) satisfy the Gaussian innovation hypotheses, and \(X_0\) has law \(\mu_0\). By the identification of the particle update with the Langevin update for \(V_N\) at step \(h=\gamma/N\) and of the square-integrable chain with the pointwise one, \(\tilde Z_k((x,y),s)=\Phi_k(x,(\hat\xi_n(s))_n)\) for \(\tilde{\mathbb P}\)-almost every \(((x,y),s)\). This depends on \(((x,y),s)\) only through \((x,s)\), and the image of \(c\otimes Q\) under \(((x,y),s)\mapsto(x,s)\) is \(\mu_0\otimes Q\) (the first marginal of \(c\) is \(\mu_0\)). The right side depends on \(\mu_0\), \(Q\), \(B\) and \(h\), but not on \(\pi\) or on the coupling \(c\). No stationarity of a reference process is involved; the coupling only serves to place a second initial point \(y\sim\pi\), correlated with \(x\), on the same probability space.

steps.title: The particle laws are the iterates of the Langevin transition
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(\mathcal N(0,I_D)\) be the standard Gaussian measure on \(\mathcal Z\), the law of a vector with independent \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) coordinates. For \(s\in\mathbb R\) and a probability measure \(\nu\) on \(\mathcal Z\), the Langevin transition is

\[K_s\nu=F_\#\bigl(\nu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I_D)\bigr),\qquad F(z,u)=z-s\nabla V_N(z)+\sqrt{2s}\,u .\]

Claim. Let \(\mathbb P\) be a probability measure, \(U\) differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\), and let \(Z_0,\xi_0,\xi_1,\dots\) satisfy the Gaussian innovation hypotheses. Then for every \(k\),

\[\rho_k=K_{\gamma/N}^{\,k}\,\mu_0,\qquad\mu_0=(Z_0)_\#\mathbb P .\]

Proof. Vector form of the hypotheses. By the section on the algorithm law, the path \((\xi_n)_n\) has law \(\mathcal G=\operatorname{pack}_\#\bigotimes_{(n,a)}\mathcal N(0,1)\). The image of \(\mathcal G\) under \((u_n)_n\mapsto u_k\) is \(\bigotimes_{a\in I}\mathcal N(0,1)=\mathcal N(0,I_D)\), so each \(\xi_k\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,I_D)\); and \(\mathcal G\) is the product of these laws, so the vectors \(\xi_0,\xi_1,\dots\) are independent.

Independence of the current state and the next innovation. Put \(s=\gamma/N\). By the dynamics section, \(Z_k=\Phi_k(Z_0,\xi_0,\dots,\xi_{k-1})\) almost surely, with \(\Phi_k\) measurable. For Borel sets \(A\), \(B\), \(C\), condition 3 and the independence of the vectors give

\[\begin{gathered}\mathbb P\bigl(Z_0\in A,(\xi_n)_{n<k}\in B,\xi_k\in C\bigr)\\=\mathbb P(Z_0\in A)\,\mathbb P\bigl((\xi_n)_{n<k}\in B\bigr)\,\mathbb P(\xi_k\in C)\\=\mathbb P\bigl(Z_0\in A,(\xi_n)_{n<k}\in B\bigr)\,\mathbb P(\xi_k\in C).\end{gathered}\]

Products \(A\times B\) form a \(\pi\)-system generating the product \(\sigma\)-algebra, so \((Z_0,\xi_0,\dots,\xi_{k-1})\) is independent of \(\xi_k\), and therefore so is the function \(Z_k\). Hence the pair \((Z_k,\xi_k)\) has law \(\rho_k\otimes\mathcal N(0,I_D)\).

Induction. For \(k=0\) the claim is \(\rho_0=\mu_0\). If \(\rho_k=K_s^k\mu_0\), then \(Z_{k+1}=F(Z_k,\xi_k)\) almost surely and

\[\rho_{k+1}=F_\#\bigl((Z_k,\xi_k)_\#\mathbb P\bigr)=F_\#\bigl(\rho_k\otimes\mathcal N(0,I_D)\bigr)=K_s\rho_k=K_s^{k+1}\mu_0 .\qquad\square\]

Thus every statement about the Langevin Markov chain for \(V_N\) at step \(\gamma/N\), started from \(\mu_0\), applies to the particle algorithm. In particular the finiteness of the transport distance between \(\rho_k\) and the Gibbs target, proved in the Langevin library for this chain, transfers to \(\rho_k\) in the proof of the main theorem.

IPLA/Generator.lean.title: The physical-time generator and the infinitesimal invariance of the target
IPLA/Generator.lean.summary:
In physical time the interacting particle algorithm discretizes the diffusion

\[dZ_t=- rac1N abla V_N(Z_t)\,dt+\sqrt{ rac2N}\,dB_t\]

on the scaled state space \(\mathcal Z\): its Euler scheme with step \(\gamma\) is the update \(Z_{k+1}=Z_k- rac\gamma N abla V_N(Z_k)+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,\xi_k\). This diffusion is the Langevin diffusion \(dY_s=- abla V_N(Y_s)\,ds+\sqrt2\,dB_s\) run at the slower clock \(s=t/N\), so its generator is \(\mathcal A_N= rac1N\mathcal L_{V_N}\), where \(\mathcal L_V\varphi=\Delta\varphi-\langle abla V, abla\varphi angle\) is the Langevin generator. This section defines \(\mathcal A_N\), proves the displayed formula for \(C^2\) test functions, and proves that the target \(\Pi_N\) is infinitesimally invariant: for every compactly supported \(C^2\) function \(\varphi\), \(\mathcal A_N\varphi\) is \(\Pi_N\)-integrable and \(\int\mathcal A_N\varphi\,d\Pi_N=0\). Only the hypotheses of the main theorem on the joint potential \(U\) are used; no second derivative of \(U\) appears. The result is not used in the proof of the main theorem, where the stationarity of the Langevin reference process is obtained by a different argument.

steps.title: The generator in physical time
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(e_1,\dots,e_D\) be an orthonormal basis of \(\mathcal Z\), \(D=d_ heta+Nd_x\). For \(W,\varphi:\mathcal Z o\mathbb R\) and \(z\in\mathcal Z\), the Langevin generator is

\[\mathcal L_W\varphi(z)=\sum_{r=1}^D\Bigl(\partial_{e_r} igl(\partial_{e_r}\varphi igr)(z)-\langle abla W(z),e_r angle\,\partial_{e_r}\varphi(z)\Bigr),\]

where \(\partial_v\) is the directional derivative \(D(\cdot)v\). The physical-time generator of the particle diffusion is \(\mathcal A_N\varphi(z)= rac1N\,\mathcal L_{V_N}\varphi(z)\), with the convention \( rac10=0\). Here \( abla V_N(z)\) denotes the gradient of \(V_N\) at \(z\) (taken to be \(0\) at a point where \(V_N\) is not differentiable; in all applications \(V_N\) is differentiable).

Claim. For every \(U\), every twice continuously differentiable \(\varphi:\mathcal Z o\mathbb R\) and every \(z\),

\[\mathcal A_N\varphi(z)= rac1N\Bigl(\Delta\varphi(z)- igl\langle abla V_N(z), abla\varphi(z) igr angle\Bigr),\qquad\Delta\varphi(z)=\sum_{r=1}^DD^2\varphi(z)(e_r,e_r).\]

Proof. Since \(\varphi\) is \(C^2\), the map \(z\mapsto D\varphi(z)\) is differentiable and the derivative of \(z\mapsto D\varphi(z)e_r\) in direction \(e_r\) is the second derivative \(D^2\varphi(z)(e_r,e_r)\). Summing over \(r\) gives the Laplacian \(\Delta\varphi(z)\), the trace of the second derivative (which does not depend on the choice of orthonormal basis). For the first-order terms, \(\partial_{e_r}\varphi(z)=\langle abla\varphi(z),e_r angle\) by the definition of the gradient, and by Parseval's identity in the orthonormal basis

\[\sum_{r=1}^D\langle abla V_N(z),e_r angle\langle abla\varphi(z),e_r angle=\langle abla V_N(z), abla\varphi(z) angle .\]

Subtracting and multiplying by \( rac1N\) gives the claim. \(\square\)

The first-order term is an algebraic identity for the vector \( abla V_N(z)\), so no regularity of \(U\) is needed for the formula. In physical coordinates the drift term is \( rac1N\langle\sum_i abla_ heta U( heta,x^i), abla_ heta\varphi angle+\sum_i\langle abla_xU( heta,x^i), rac1{\sqrt N} abla_{z_i}\varphi angle\), the generator of the parameter moving along the average force with diffusion coefficient \(2/N\) and of each particle performing a Langevin diffusion in its pair potential.

steps.title: Infinitesimal invariance of the Gibbs target
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(N\ge1\), \(m>0\), \(L\ge0\), and let the joint potential \(U=U_y\) (for a fixed datum \(y\)) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Then \(\Pi_N\) is a probability measure, and for every twice continuously differentiable \(\varphi:\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R\) with compact support,

\[\mathcal A_N\varphi\in L^1(\Pi_N)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\int_{\mathcal Z}\mathcal A_N\varphi\,d\Pi_N=0 .\]

Proof. The probability property was proved in the section on foundations. Put \(W=V_N\); it is differentiable and \(\nabla W\) is \(NL\)-Lipschitz, in particular continuous, by the geometry section. Let \(K\) be the compact support of \(\varphi\) and fix a basis vector \(v=e_r\).

Integrability. The function \(f_v=e^{-W}\bigl(\partial_v\partial_v\varphi-\langle\nabla W,v\rangle\partial_v\varphi\bigr)\) vanishes outside \(K\), because all derivatives of \(\varphi\) vanish on the open complement of the support. On \(K\) it is continuous, hence bounded. A bounded measurable function with compact support is Lebesgue integrable, so \(f_v\in L^1(dz)\). Since \(\Pi_N\) has density \(e^{-W}/Z_N\) with \(0<Z_N<\infty\), \(\int|\mathcal L_W\varphi|\,d\Pi_N\le Z_N^{-1}\sum_r\int|f_{e_r}|\,dz<\infty\), and multiplying by \(\frac1N\) preserves integrability.

Integration by parts. The function \(g_v=e^{-W}\partial_v\varphi\) is differentiable with compact support in \(K\), and by the product and chain rules

\[\partial_vg_v=e^{-W}\partial_v\partial_v\varphi-e^{-W}\langle\nabla W,v\rangle\partial_v\varphi=f_v .\]

Choose orthonormal coordinates with \(v\) as the first axis. By Fubini's theorem (applicable since \(f_v\) is integrable) and the fundamental theorem of calculus on each line parallel to \(v\), \(\int f_v\,dz=\int\bigl(\int_{\mathbb R}\partial_tg_v(z'+tv)\,dt\bigr)dz'=0\), because \(t\mapsto g_v(z'+tv)\) vanishes for \(|t|\) large. Summing over \(r\) gives \(\int e^{-W}\mathcal L_W\varphi\,dz=0\).

Conclusion. \(\int\mathcal L_W\varphi\,d\Pi_N=Z_N^{-1}\int e^{-W}\mathcal L_W\varphi\,dz=0\), and therefore \(\int\mathcal A_N\varphi\,d\Pi_N=\frac1N\cdot0=0\). \(\square\)

The integrability statement is part of the conclusion, so the vanishing integral is a genuine computation. Only the first derivative of \(U\), through \(\nabla V_N\), enters; no Hessian of \(U\) is assumed. Infinitesimal invariance concerns the generator on test functions; that the law of a solution of the diffusion started at \(\Pi_N\) stays equal to \(\Pi_N\) is a different statement, proved for the Langevin reference process in the Langevin library.

IPLA/Degenerate.lean.title: Zero-dimensional parameter and state spaces
IPLA/Degenerate.lean.summary: The main theorem allows \(d_\theta=0\) and \(d_x=0\). The space \(\mathbb R^0\) consists of the single vector \(0\), and this section records the two consequences used for these degenerate dimensions: if \(d_\theta=0\), the parameter error \(\bigl(\int\|P_\theta z-\theta_\star\|^2\,d\nu(z)\bigr)^{1/2}\) vanishes for every measure \(\nu\) and every \(\theta_\star\); and if \(d_\theta=d_x=0\), the state space \(\mathcal Z\) is a single point, the Wasserstein distance between any two probability measures on it vanishes, and the error bound of the main theorem reduces to \(0\le0\). No hypothesis on the potential, the innovations or the initial state is needed. The main theorem treats the case of an empty coordinate set (\(d_\theta=d_x=0\)) by the second result and all other cases by the general argument.

steps.title: No parameter error in parameter dimension zero
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(d_\theta=0\), let \(N,d_x\in\mathbb N\) be arbitrary, let \(\nu\) be any measure on \(\mathcal Z=\mathbb R^0\times(\mathbb R^{d_x})^N\) and \(\theta_\star\in\mathbb R^0\). Then

\[\Bigl(\int_{\mathcal Z}\|P_\theta z-\theta_\star\|^2\,d\nu(z)\Bigr)^{1/2}=0 .\]

Proof. The space \(\mathbb R^0\) has exactly one element, so \(P_\theta z=\theta_\star\) for every \(z\). Hence \(\|P_\theta z-\theta_\star\|^2=\|0\|^2=0\) for every \(z\), the integral of the zero function is \(0\) for any measure, and \(\sqrt0=0\). \(\square\)

The latent blocks may be nontrivial: the algorithm can move the particles, but its projected parameter error is identically zero.

steps.title: The error bound on a one-point state space
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(d_\theta=d_x=0\) and \(N\in\mathbb N\), so that \(\mathcal Z=\mathbb R^0\) is a single point. Let \(\mu,\pi\) be probability measures and \(\nu\) any measure on \(\mathcal Z\), let \(m,\gamma\in\mathbb R\), \(L\ge0\), \(\theta_\star\in\mathbb R^0\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\). Then, with the conventions \(a/0=0\) and \(\sqrt a=0\) for \(a<0\),

\[\Bigl(\int\|P_\theta z-\theta_\star\|^2\,d\nu\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac{2\cdot0}{Nm}}+(1-m\gamma)^k\,W_2(\mu,\pi)+\frac{33}{20}\,\frac Lm\,\sqrt{0+\frac0N}\,\sqrt\gamma .\]

Proof. The left side is \(0\) by the previous step. On the right, \(\sqrt{0/(Nm)}=\sqrt0=0\) and \(\sqrt{0+0/N}=0\). Finally \(W_2(\mu,\pi)=0\): the product measure \(\mu\otimes\pi\) is a coupling of \(\mu\) and \(\pi\), it is carried by the single point \((z,z)\) of \(\mathcal Z\times\mathcal Z\), and its cost \(\int\|x-y\|^2\,d(\mu\otimes\pi)\) is \(0\); since \(W_2\ge0\) is the infimum of the costs, it equals \(0\). The right side is therefore \(0+(1-m\gamma)^k\cdot0+0=0\), and the claim is \(0\le0\). \(\square\)

The displayed right side is the bound of the main theorem with \(d_\theta=d_x=0\). The inequality holds without any assumption on \(m\), \(\gamma\), \(L\), the potential, the innovations or the measures beyond \(\mu(\mathcal Z)=\pi(\mathcal Z)=1\), which is needed for the product coupling to have the prescribed marginals.

IPLA/MarginalConcentration.lean.title: The marginal density, its maximizer and the parameter marginal of the target
IPLA/MarginalConcentration.lean.summary:
Throughout, \(U\) is the joint potential on \(\mathcal J=\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_x}\), assumed differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\), and \(\ell(\theta)=\int e^{-U(\theta,x)}\,dx\in[0,\infty]\) is its marginal density. This section proves, from these two hypotheses only:

  • a Gaussian bound \(e^{-U(\theta,x)}\le C_Ue^{-\frac m4\|\theta\|^2}e^{-\frac m4\|x\|^2}\), with \(C_U=\exp(\|\nabla U(0)\|^2/m-U(0))\);
  • \(0<\ell(\theta)<\infty\) for every \(\theta\), \(\ell\) is continuous, and \(\ell(\theta)\to0\) as \(\|\theta\|\to\infty\); consequently a marginal maximizer \(\theta_\star\) exists;
  • for \(N\ge1\), the image of the Gibbs target \(\Pi_N\) under the parameter projection \(P_\theta\) is the probability measure
\[\pi_N^\theta(d\theta)=\frac{\ell(\theta)^N\,d\theta}{\int_{\mathbb R^{d_\theta}}\ell(u)^N\,du},\qquad0<\int\ell^N<\infty,\qquad\int\|\theta\|^2\,d\pi_N^\theta<\infty .\]

The last identity is the reason why the interacting particle algorithm estimates a marginal maximizer: under the target, the parameter has density proportional to the \(N\)-th power of the marginal likelihood. Its proof integrates out the \(N\) latent blocks: with \(x^i=\sqrt Nz_i\), the latent integral of \(e^{-V_N}\) at fixed \(\theta\) factorizes into \(N\) copies of \(\ell(\theta)\), multiplied by the Jacobian \(N^{-Nd_x/2}\) of the dilation; this constant and the constant from the regrouping of coordinates do not depend on \(\theta\) and cancel after normalization. All integrals are taken in \([0,\infty]\) until finiteness has been proved. Strong convexity of \(-\log\ell\) and the concentration of \(\pi_N^\theta\) are proved in the following sections.

steps.title: The norm of a parameter–latent pair
steps.body:
Claim. For \(\theta\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^{d_x}\), the pair \((\theta,x)\in\mathcal J\) has parameter coordinates \(\theta_j\) and latent coordinates \(x_j\), and

\[\|(\theta,x)\|^2=\|\theta\|^2+\|x\|^2 .\qquad(1)\]

Moreover the map \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_x}\to\mathcal J\), \((\theta,x)\mapsto(\theta,x)\), is continuous (for the product topology on the left).

Proof. The coordinate formulas hold by definition of the pair. The squared Euclidean norm of \((\theta,x)\) is the sum of the squares of its coordinates; splitting this sum over the parameter indices and the latent indices gives \(\sum_j\theta_j^2+\sum_jx_j^2=\|\theta\|^2+\|x\|^2\). A map into the Euclidean space \(\mathcal J\) is continuous if each of its finitely many coordinates is continuous, and each coordinate of the pair is a coordinate projection of \(\theta\) or of \(x\), which is continuous. \(\square\)

By (1), a Gaussian factor in the joint norm splits into a parameter factor and a latent factor, and continuity of \(U\) gives continuity of \((\theta,x)\mapsto U(\theta,x)\) and of its slices.

Claim. Let \(m>0\) and let \(U\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex. Then for all \(\theta\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^{d_x}\),

\[e^{-U(\theta,x)}\le C_U\,e^{-a\|\theta\|^2}\,e^{-a\|x\|^2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bigl|e^{-U(\theta,x)}\bigr|\le C_U\,e^{-a\|x\|^2},\qquad(2)\]

and for every \(\theta\) the function \(x\mapsto e^{-U(\theta,x)}\) is Lebesgue integrable on \(\mathbb R^{d_x}\).

\[U(v)\ge U(0)-\frac{\|\nabla U(0)\|^2}m+\frac m4\|v\|^2 .\]

steps.title: Finiteness, positivity and continuity of the marginal density
steps.body:
For each \(\theta\), let \(\lambda(\theta)=\int_{\mathbb R^{d_x}}e^{-U(\theta,x)}\,dx\in\mathbb R\) be the Lebesgue integral of the integrable function of the previous step.

Claim. Let \(m>0\) and let \(U\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex. Then for every \(\theta\),

\[\ell(\theta)=\lambda(\theta),\qquad0<\ell(\theta)<\infty,\]

and both \(\lambda:\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\to\mathbb R\) and \(\ell:\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\to[0,\infty]\) are continuous.

Proof. Equality and finiteness. For a nonnegative integrable function, the integral computed in \([0,\infty]\) equals its Lebesgue integral, which is a finite real number. Applied to \(x\mapsto e^{-U(\theta,x)}\), this gives \(\ell(\theta)=\lambda(\theta)<\infty\).

Positivity. The integrand is strictly positive everywhere. If its integral were \(0\), the nonnegative integrand would vanish almost everywhere, which is impossible because Lebesgue measure of \(\mathbb R^{d_x}\) is positive. Hence \(\lambda(\theta)>0\).

Continuity. Let \(\theta_n\to\theta\). For each \(x\), \(e^{-U(\theta_n,x)}\to e^{-U(\theta,x)}\) because \(U\) and the pairing are continuous. By (2) all integrands are bounded by \(C_Ue^{-a\|x\|^2}\), which is integrable and independent of \(n\). The dominated convergence theorem gives \(\lambda(\theta_n)\to\lambda(\theta)\); since \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\) is a metric space, sequential continuity is continuity. Finally \(\ell\) is the composition of \(\lambda\) with the continuous inclusion \([0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]\). \(\square\)

Thus the marginal density of the definition is a continuous, finite and positive function, and \(-\log\ell\) is a real-valued function; a maximizer of \(\ell\) cannot have infinite marginal likelihood.

steps.title: Decay at infinity and existence of a marginal maximizer
steps.body:
Put \(G=\int_{\mathbb R^{d_x}}e^{-a\|x\|^2}\,dx<\infty\).

Claim. Let \(m>0\) and let \(U\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex. Then

(a) \(\lambda(\theta)\le C_U\,G\,e^{-a\|\theta\|^2}\) for every \(\theta\);

(b) \(\lambda(\theta)\to0\) as \(\theta\) leaves every compact set, i.e. for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a compact \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\) with \(\lambda(\theta)<\varepsilon\) for \(\theta\notin K\);

(c) there exists a marginal maximizer: some \(\theta_\star\) satisfies \(\ell(\theta)\le\ell(\theta_\star)\) for all \(\theta\).

Proof. (a) Integrate the first inequality of (2) in \(x\): both sides are integrable, the integral is monotone, and the factor \(C_Ue^{-a\|\theta\|^2}\) does not depend on \(x\).

(b) Let \(\varepsilon>0\). Since \(C_UGe^{-ar^2}\to0\) as \(r\to\infty\), there is \(R\) with \(C_UGe^{-a\|\theta\|^2}<\varepsilon\) whenever \(\|\theta\|>R\). The closed ball \(K=\{\|\theta\|\le R\}\) is compact in finite dimension, and by (a) and \(\lambda\ge0\), \(0\le\lambda(\theta)<\varepsilon\) for \(\theta\notin K\).

(c) By the previous step \(\lambda(0)>0\). By (b) with \(\varepsilon=\lambda(0)\) there is a compact \(K\) with \(\lambda(\theta)<\lambda(0)\) for \(\theta\notin K\). The set \(K'=K\cup\{0\}\) is compact and nonempty and \(\lambda\) is continuous, so by the extreme value theorem \(\lambda\) attains its maximum over \(K'\) at some \(\theta_\star\in K'\). For \(\theta\in K'\), \(\lambda(\theta)\le\lambda(\theta_\star)\); for \(\theta\notin K'\), \(\lambda(\theta)<\lambda(0)\le\lambda(\theta_\star)\). Thus \(\theta_\star\) maximizes \(\lambda\) on \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\). Since \(\ell=\lambda\) and the inclusion \([0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]\) is monotone, \(\ell(\theta)\le\ell(\theta_\star)\) for all \(\theta\). \(\square\)

No differentiability of \(\ell\) is used. If \(d_\theta=0\) the parameter space is a point and (c) is trivial. Uniqueness of the maximizer is proved in the section on strong log-concavity.

steps.title: Product integrals and the dilation of the latent blocks
steps.body:
Claim. (a) Let \(\mu\) be a \(\sigma\)-finite measure on a measurable space \(E\), \(f:E\to[0,\infty]\) measurable and \(n\in\mathbb N\). Then

\[\int_{E^n}\prod_{i=1}^nf(x_i)\,d\mu^{\otimes n}(x)=\Bigl(\int_Ef\,d\mu\Bigr)^n\quad\text{in }[0,\infty].\]

(b) Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real normed space of dimension \(d\) with an additive Haar measure \(\mu\) (for instance Lebesgue measure), \(f:E\to[0,\infty]\) measurable and \(r\ne0\). Then \(\int f(rx)\,d\mu(x)=|r^d|^{-1}\int f\,d\mu\).

(c) Let \(N\ge1\), let \(U\) be differentiable and \(\theta\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\). Then

\[\int_{(\mathbb R^{d_x})^N}\prod_{i=1}^Ne^{-U(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)}\,dz_1\cdots dz_N=\Bigl(\bigl|(\sqrt N)^{d_x}\bigr|^{-1}\,\ell(\theta)\Bigr)^N=N^{-Nd_x/2}\,\ell(\theta)^N\quad\text{in }[0,\infty].\]

Proof. (a) Induction on \(n\). For \(n=0\), \(E^0\) is a single point, \(\mu^{\otimes0}\) is the unit point mass and the empty product equals \(1\), so both sides equal \(1\). For the inductive step, the map \(x\mapsto(x_1,(x_2,\dots,x_{n+1}))\) carries \(\mu^{\otimes(n+1)}\) to \(\mu\otimes\mu^{\otimes n}\), so the integral over \(E^{n+1}\) equals the integral over \(E\times E^n\) of \(f(x_1)\cdot\prod_{i=2}^{n+1}f(x_i)\). By Tonelli's theorem, the integral of a product of a nonnegative function of the first variable and one of the second is the product of the integrals; by the induction hypothesis this is \(\bigl(\int f\bigr)\bigl(\int f\bigr)^n=\bigl(\int f\bigr)^{n+1}\). No finiteness is needed, since Tonelli's theorem holds in \([0,\infty]\).

(b) The image of \(\mu\) under \(x\mapsto rx\) is \(|r^d|^{-1}\mu\): it is again translation invariant, and it gives the unit-scaled sets the mass \(\mu(r^{-1}A)=|r|^{-d}\mu(A)\). By the change-of-variables formula for image measures, \(\int f(rx)\,d\mu(x)=\int f\,d(r\cdot)_\#\mu=|r^d|^{-1}\int f\,d\mu\).

(c) Lebesgue measure on \((\mathbb R^{d_x})^N\) is the \(N\)-fold product of Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb R^{d_x}\). The function \(f(z)=e^{-U(\theta,\sqrt Nz)}\) is continuous, hence measurable, and (a) gives \(\bigl(\int f\bigr)^N\). By (b) with \(r=\sqrt N\ne0\) (as \(N\ge1\)) and \(d=d_x\), \(\int f=|(\sqrt N)^{d_x}|^{-1}\int e^{-U(\theta,x)}dx=|(\sqrt N)^{d_x}|^{-1}\ell(\theta)\). \(\square\)

With \(x^i=\sqrt Nz_i\), (c) is the latent integral of the Gibbs weight at a fixed parameter: the substitution in each of the \(N\) blocks produces the factor \(N^{-d_x/2}\), and the blocks contribute independent copies of \(\ell(\theta)\). The constant \(N^{-Nd_x/2}\in(0,\infty)\) does not depend on \(\theta\). No convexity is used in this step.

steps.title: Regrouping the state into parameter and particle blocks
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(\Theta=\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\) and \(\mathcal X=(\mathbb R^{d_x})^N\), with elements \((z_i)_{i=1}^N\). Define \(C:\Theta\times\mathcal X\to\mathcal Z\) by letting \(C(\theta,(z_i)_i)\) be the state with parameter block \(\theta\) and latent blocks \(z_1,\dots,z_N\), that is, \(C(\theta,z)_{(\theta,j)}=\theta_j\) and \(C(\theta,z)_{(i,j)}=z_{i,j}\).

Claim. \(C\) is a linear bijection, with inverse \(w\mapsto(P_\theta w,(w_i)_{i=1}^N)\), and both \(C\) and its inverse are continuous. Moreover, for all \(\theta\), \(z\) and \(i\),

\[P_\theta\,C(\theta,z)=\theta,\qquad J_i\,C(\theta,z)=\bigl(\theta,\sqrt N\,z_i\bigr).\]

Proof. All statements are checked coordinatewise. The coordinates of \(C(\theta,z)\) are coordinates of \(\theta\) or of \(z\), so \(C\) is linear. Applying \(C\) after \(w\mapsto(P_\theta w,(w_i)_i)\) returns each coordinate of \(w\), and applying the inverse map after \(C\) returns \(\theta\) and each block \(z_i\); hence the two maps are mutually inverse. Linear maps between finite-dimensional spaces are continuous. The parameter coordinates of \(C(\theta,z)\) are those of \(\theta\), which gives \(P_\theta C(\theta,z)=\theta\); and the pair extraction \(J_i\) takes the parameter block and \(\sqrt N\) times block \(i\), which gives the last identity. \(\square\)

The map \(C\) is the change of variables that lets the parameter and the latent blocks be integrated separately, as in the product integrals of the previous step.

For a measure \(\mu\) and a measurable \(w\ge0\), \(w\cdot\mu\) denotes the measure \(A\mapsto\int_Aw\,d\mu\).

Claim. (a) For all \(\theta\) and \(z=(z_i)_i\), \(e^{-V_N(C(\theta,z))}=\prod_{i=1}^Ne^{-U(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)}\).

(b) Let \(e:A\to B\) be a measurable bijection with measurable inverse, \(\mu\) a measure on \(A\) and \(w:B\to[0,\infty]\) measurable. Then \(e_\#\bigl((w\circ e)\cdot\mu\bigr)=w\cdot(e_\#\mu)\).

(c) Let \(\mu\) be a measure on \(A\), \(\nu\) an s-finite measure on \(B\) (a countable sum of finite measures; every \(\sigma\)-finite measure is s-finite) and \(w:A\times B\to[0,\infty]\) measurable. Then the image of \(w\cdot(\mu\otimes\nu)\) under the first projection is \(\bigl(\theta\mapsto\int_Bw(\theta,x)\,d\nu(x)\bigr)\cdot\mu\).

Proof. (a) By the previous step \(J_iC(\theta,z)=(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)\), so \(V_N(C(\theta,z))=\sum_iU(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)\), and \(e^{-\sum_it_i}=\prod_ie^{-t_i}\). The values are positive reals, and the product in \([0,\infty]\) of nonnegative reals is their ordinary product.

(b) Let \(S\subseteq B\) be measurable. By definition of the image measure and of the density, and by the change-of-variables formula \(\int g\circ e\,d\mu=\int g\,d(e_\#\mu)\) for measurable \(g\ge0\),

\[e_\#\bigl((w\circ e)\cdot\mu\bigr)(S)=\int_A\mathbf 1_S(e(a))\,w(e(a))\,d\mu(a)=\int_B\mathbf 1_S\,w\,d(e_\#\mu)=\bigl(w\cdot e_\#\mu\bigr)(S).\]

(c) Let \(S\subseteq A\) be measurable. The preimage of \(S\) under the first projection is \(S\times B\), and by Tonelli's theorem

\[\int_{S\times B}w\,d(\mu\otimes\nu)=\int_A\mathbf 1_S(\theta)\Bigl(\int_Bw(\theta,x)\,d\nu(x)\Bigr)d\mu(\theta).\]

The left side is the image measure of \(S\) and the right side is the measure of \(S\) with density \(\theta\mapsto\int w(\theta,x)\,d\nu(x)\). Two measures that agree on all measurable sets are equal. \(\square\)
