Definition. For \(N\in\mathbb N\), the marginal target is the measure on \(\Theta=\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\)

\[\pi_N^\theta=\Bigl(\int_\Theta\ell(u)^N\,du\Bigr)^{-1}\,\ell^N\cdot\mathrm{Leb}_\Theta,\]

computed in \([0,\infty]\).

Claim. Let \(N\ge1\), \(m>0\), and let \(U\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex. Then \((P_\theta)_\#\Pi_N=\pi_N^\theta\).

Proof. Let \(w=e^{-V_N}\), \(\mu=w\cdot\mathrm{Leb}_{\mathcal Z}\) (so that \(\Pi_N=\mu(\mathcal Z)^{-1}\mu\)), \(\rho=\ell^N\cdot\mathrm{Leb}_\Theta\) and \(\kappa=|(\sqrt N)^{d_x}|^{-1}\in(0,\infty)\). The functions \(w\) and \(\ell^N\) are measurable, being continuous (for \(\ell\) by the continuity step, which uses strong convexity), and \(C\), \(P_\theta\) are continuous, hence measurable.

Step 1. By the regrouping-volume identity, \(C_\#\mathrm{Leb}_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}=c\,\mathrm{Leb}_{\mathcal Z}\) with \(0<c<\infty\). By identity (b) of the previous step but one, applied to \(e=C\),

\[C_\#\bigl((w\circ C)\cdot\mathrm{Leb}_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}\bigr)=w\cdot C_\#\mathrm{Leb}_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}=c\,\mu .\]

Step 2. Since \(P_\theta\circ C\) is the first projection and images compose,

\[c\,(P_\theta)_\#\mu=(P_\theta)_\#(c\mu)=(P_\theta\circ C)_\#\bigl((w\circ C)\cdot\mathrm{Leb}_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}\bigr)=\Bigl(\theta\mapsto\int_{\mathcal X}w(C(\theta,z))\,dz\Bigr)\cdot\mathrm{Leb}_\Theta\]

by identity (c) of that step (Lebesgue measure on \(\Theta\times\mathcal X\) is the product measure).

Step 3. By the factorization (a) and the product-integral formula, \(\int_{\mathcal X}w(C(\theta,z))\,dz=\int\prod_ie^{-U(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)}\,dz=\kappa^N\ell(\theta)^N\). Hence \(c\,(P_\theta)_\#\mu=\kappa^N\rho\).

Step 4. Normalize both sides. Since \(c\) and \(\kappa^N\) lie in \((0,\infty)\), the cancellation identity gives

\[\bigl((P_\theta)_\#\mu(\Theta)\bigr)^{-1}(P_\theta)_\#\mu=\rho(\Theta)^{-1}\rho=\pi_N^\theta .\]

Finally \((P_\theta)_\#\mu(\Theta)=\mu(P_\theta^{-1}(\Theta))=\mu(\mathcal Z)\), and the image of a scalar multiple is the scalar multiple of the image, so the left side is \((P_\theta)_\#\bigl(\mu(\mathcal Z)^{-1}\mu\bigr)=(P_\theta)_\#\Pi_N\). \(\square\)

The identity is an equality of measures in \([0,\infty]\)-valued arithmetic and does not use the finiteness of any normalizing constant. In words: under the target \(\Pi_N\), the parameter has density proportional to \(\ell(\theta)^N\). Since \(\ell>0\) and \(t\mapsto t^N\) is increasing, the maximizers of this density are exactly the marginal maximizers, and the density concentrates around them as \(N\) grows.

steps.title: The marginal target is a probability measure with finite second moment
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(m>0\) and let \(U\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex.

(a) If \(N\ge1\), then \(\pi_N^\theta\) is a probability measure.

(b) For every \(N\in\mathbb N\), \(\int_\Theta\ell(\theta)^N\,d\theta>0\).

(c) If \(N\ge1\), then \(\int_\Theta\ell(\theta)^N\,d\theta<\infty\).

(d) If \(N\ge1\), then \(\int\|\theta\|^2\,d\pi_N^\theta(\theta)<\infty\).

Proof. (a) \(\Pi_N\) is a probability measure by the section on foundations. By the previous step and the definition of the image measure, \(\pi_N^\theta(\Theta)=\Pi_N(P_\theta^{-1}(\Theta))=\Pi_N(\mathcal Z)=1\).

(b) The function \(\ell^N\) is measurable (continuous) and nowhere zero, because \(\ell(\theta)>0\). For a measurable function \(f\ge0\), \(\int f\,d\mathrm{Leb}>0\) if and only if the set \(\{f\ne0\}\) has positive measure; here that set is \(\Theta\), whose Lebesgue measure is positive.

(c) Suppose \(\int\ell^N=\infty\). Then its inverse is \(0\) and \(\pi_N^\theta=0\cdot(\ell^N\cdot\mathrm{Leb})=0\), so \(\pi_N^\theta(\Theta)=0\), contradicting (a).

(d) By the previous step and the change-of-variables formula for image measures, \(\int\|\theta\|^2d\pi_N^\theta=\int\|P_\theta z\|^2d\Pi_N(z)\le\int\|z\|^2d\Pi_N(z)\), using \(\|P_\theta z\|\le\|z\|\). The right side is finite by the section on foundations. \(\square\)

By (b) and (c) the normalizing constant of \(\pi_N^\theta\) is a positive real number, so \(\pi_N^\theta\) has the ordinary probability density \(\ell^N/\int\ell^N\). Finiteness in (c) is deduced from the projection identity, not from a separate estimate of \(\ell^N\).

IPLA/PrekopaLeindler.lean.title: One-dimensional Prékopa–Leindler inequality
IPLA/PrekopaLeindler.lean.summary: Let the two one-dimensional densities be continuous, strictly positive, and have finite positive integrals. Their cumulative distribution functions define an increasing transport map. Its derivative, together with the weighted arithmetic–geometric mean inequality and change of variables, proves the normalized Prékopa–Leindler inequality. Rescaling the densities proves the inequality for arbitrary finite positive masses.

steps.title: Differentiability and strict increase of the cumulative integral
steps.body:
Let \(f\) be continuous, strictly positive, and integrable on \(\mathbb R\), with \(\int f=1\). Its cumulative distribution function is \(F(x)=\int_{(-\infty,x]}f\). Splitting the integral at zero gives

\[F(y)-F(0)=\int_0^y f(t)dt\]

The fundamental theorem of calculus gives \(F'(x)=f(x)\). Thus the cumulative function is differentiable and continuous. For \(y>x\), the difference \(F(y)-F(x)=\int_x^y f(t)dt\) is positive because a positive continuous function has positive integral on a nonempty interval. Consequently the cumulative function is strictly increasing. The infinite lower limit is constant in the local differentiation argument.

steps.title: The cumulative range and the open unit interval
steps.body:
Integrability gives \(F(x)\to0\) as \(x\to-\infty\). Splitting the unit integral at \(x\) gives \(F(x)=1-\int_{(x,\infty)}f\), hence \(F(x)\to1\) as \(x\to+\infty\). Positivity first gives \(0\le F\le1\). Strict monotonicity, applied at \(x\) and its neighboring points \(x-1\) and \(x+1\), then gives \(0<F(x)<1\).

For any \(u\in(0,1)\), the endpoint limits supply two finite arguments whose cumulative values lie below and above \(u\). Continuity gives an argument with \(F(x)=u\), and strict monotonicity makes it unique. Therefore \(F(\mathbb R)=(0,1)\). The inverse cumulative function is consequently defined exactly on the open unit interval; neither endpoint is attained at a finite argument.

steps.title: The increasing transport map and its derivative
steps.body:
For cumulative distribution functions \(F,G\), define \(T=G^{-1}\circ F\). Both have range \((0,1)\), so \(G(T(x))=F(x)\). Strict monotonicity makes \(G\) injective, and \(G'(T(x))=g(T(x))>0\) permits the inverse-function theorem. The chain rule gives

\[T'(x)=\frac{f(x)}{g(T(x))}>0.\]

In particular \(T\) is strictly increasing. The identity \(G(T(x))=F(x)\) equates the cumulative probabilities at corresponding arguments. Its differentiated form is \(g(T(x))T'(x)=f(x)\). The denominator is positive, so division is justified and yields the derivative and density change-of-variables relation. Both the map and its derivative follow from the density assumptions.

steps.title: Change of variables in the normalized inequality
steps.body:
Assume \(0\le t\le1\) and the interpolation inequality \(h((1-t)x+ty)\ge f(x)^{1-t}g(y)^t\). Define \(S(x)=(1-t)x+tT(x)\) and \(r=f(x)/g(T(x))>0\). The derivative is \(S'=1-t+tr>0\). Weighted arithmetic–geometric mean gives \(r^t\le1-t+tr=S'\). Applying the interpolation inequality with \(y=T(x)\) therefore yields

\[f(x)=f(x)^{1-t}g(T(x))^t r^t\le h(S(x))S'(x).\]

The increasing map \(S\) permits change of variables. Its right-hand integral becomes the integral of \(h\) over \(S(\mathbb R)\), which is at most the integral over \(\mathbb R\) by nonnegativity. Since the first density has mass one, \(1\le\int h\). The extended nonnegative integral makes this valid without assuming integrability or continuity of \(h\).

The cancellation can also be written directly in terms of \(S(x)=(1-t)x+tT(x)\). The hypothesis gives a lower bound on \(h(S(x))\) by \(f(x)^{1-t}g(T(x))^t\); the derivative satisfies \(S'(x)=(1-t)+tT'(x)\ge T'(x)^t\). Since \(T'=f/g(T)\), multiplication gives \(h(S(x))S'(x)\ge f(x)\) and integration gives \(\int h\ge\int f=1\). For nonunit masses, divide \(f,g\) by their positive integrals; restoration of their normalizations gives the factor \((\int f)^{1-t}(\int g)^t\).

The scalar inequality \((1-t)+tr\ge r^t\) is valid for all \(r>0\) and includes \(t=0,1\). Substituting \(r=f/g(T)\) is the reason the density factors cancel after multiplication by the Jacobian. The argument integrates only over the image of the interpolating map; nonnegativity of \(h\) makes surjectivity unnecessary.

steps.title: The inequality for arbitrary positive finite masses
steps.body:
A strictly positive integrable function on a nonzero measure space has positive integral. Write \(A=\int f>0\), \(B=\int g>0\), and \(C=A^{1-t}B^t>0\). Apply the normalized result to \(f/A\), \(g/B\), and \(h/C\). The identity \(\log(f/A)=\log f-\log A\) verifies the rescaled interpolation inequality. If \(h\) is also nonnegative and integrable, the extended conclusion becomes \(1\le(\int h)/C\). Multiplication by \(C\) gives

\[\exp\!\left((1-t)\log\int f+t\log\int g\right)\le\int h.\]

Thus normalization of \(f\) and \(g\) changes the interpolation factor by \(A^{1-t}B^t\), and multiplication by that positive finite factor recovers the original statement. The logarithms occur only at positive numbers and therefore also define the formula at endpoint weights. The positivity argument applies to the one-point measure in dimension zero as well.

The coordinate insertion \((s,x)\mapsto(s,x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) is continuous. Define the first marginal by \(f_1(x)=\int_\mathbb R f(s,x)ds\). IPLA.lean.title: Interacting particle Langevin: transport and entropy convergence
IPLA.lean.summary:
The same Gaussian interacting-particle recursion admits two kinds of estimates. Joint strong convexity gives a quadratic-transport bound and parameter root mean square error about a marginal-likelihood maximizer. A logarithmic Sobolev inequality for the coupled particle target gives relative-entropy bounds for the joint and projected laws. The hypotheses, initial quantities, and particle normalizations differ and are stated separately.

The root module imports the complete particle library. It exports the strongly convex transport/RMS theorem together with the separate conditional lifted-LSI entropy route. It adds no declarations of its own; the linked dependency modules provide the detailed mathematical and Lean proofs.

steps.title: The strongly convex transport and parameter estimates
steps.body:
In scaled coordinates the summed potential has explicit curvature and gradient constants. These regularity properties normalize its Gibbs law and permit a stationary Langevin coupling for the full-state transport bound. Latent integration independently identifies the parameter Gibbs marginal and proves its concentration about the unique marginal-likelihood maximizer. Projection and Minkowski’s inequality then add equilibrium concentration to the transport estimate, giving the equilibrium, transient, and discretization terms in the parameter bound.

The imported chain begins with \(V_N(\theta,z)=\sum_iU(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)\), proves dimension \(d_\theta+Nd_x\), convexity \(Nm\) and smoothness \(NL\), identifies the Gaussian algorithm with step \(\gamma/N\), and applies shared Gaussian ULA transport. In parallel, Gaussian domination and proved Prékopa–Leindler identify the parameter target and prove its \(Nm\)-strong convexity. The final projection estimate adds equilibrium radius \(\sqrt{2d_\theta/(Nm)}\), transient transport \((1-m\gamma)^kW_2(\mu_0,\Pi_N)\), and Euler bias \((33/20)(L/m)\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma\). Root import therefore exposes a theorem whose normalization, moments, stationarity and concentration inputs have all been derived.

This entry module assembles the named proof families through imports. The complete assumptions, intermediate estimates and final conclusions are stated in the dependency pages below. Building the entry module recompiles its imported dependencies and verifies that their interfaces agree.

steps.title: The joint and parameter entropy estimates
steps.body:
The entropy estimate concerns the relative entropy of the current joint law with respect to the lifted Gibbs target. Applying data processing to both laws gives the projected parameter-law divergence. It does not by itself give concentration about a deterministic maximizing parameter. The conditional interpolation theorem and the Gaussian interpolation construction establish their respective entropy estimates under the distinct assumptions stated in each result.

The LSI imports instead assume an LSI of constant \(\beta\) for the actual \(\Pi_N\) and the regular interpolation data needed by the shared entropy proof. They prove finite actual KL and \(H_k\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+8\gamma N(d_\theta+Nd_x)L^2/\beta\), then derive normalized and parameter-projection consequences. The \(\beta=N\alpha\) specialization is explicitly additional. Run lake build IPLA and the two audit modules to check the public endpoints and their dependency chains.

IPLA/LSI/UnconditionalTheorem.lean.title: Particle-entropy convergence from the lifted logarithmic Sobolev inequality
IPLA/LSI/UnconditionalTheorem.lean.summary: The Gaussian interpolation theorem derives the required density, differentiation, and integrability properties from the entropy assumptions. For the particle model, substitute \(V_N\), step \(\gamma/N\), gradient constant \(NL\), and dimension \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\). The lifted-target logarithmic Sobolev inequality, positive admissible step, and finite initial joint entropy then imply finite output entropy and the quantitative estimate. Division by particle count and parameter projection give the stated corollaries.

steps.title: Finite joint entropy and its convergence estimate
steps.body:
Let \(N>0\), \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\), and \(V_N(z)=\sum_iU(\theta,\sqrt N z_i)\). Assume differentiability of \(U\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, a logarithmic Sobolev inequality of constant \(\beta>0\) for \(\Pi_N\), a positive physical step satisfying \(\gamma\le\beta/(4NL^2)\), and finite initial joint entropy \(H_0\). Every particle law then has finite divergence and satisfies

\[H_k\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}.\]

The lifted potential is differentiable with \(NL\)-Lipschitz gradient, and its Gaussian Euler law at step \(h=\gamma/N\) is the particle law. The physical restriction is equivalent to \(h\le\beta/(4(NL)^2)\). Thus the Gaussian interpolation theorem applies with \(h=\gamma/N\), dimension \(D\), and gradient constant \(NL\). Its rate is \(e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}\) and its error is \(8\gamma ND L^2/\beta\). The admissible positive step also gives positive \(L\) before any division.

In detail, the squared gradient constant is \(\ell^2=N^2L^2\) and the step is \(h=\gamma/N\). These substitutions give restriction \(\gamma\le\beta/(4NL^2)\) and error term \(8\gamma NDL^2/\beta\). The Gaussian theorem supplies the interpolation regularity and the compatibility of constants, so neither is an additional premise here. The finite-divergence conclusion is retained alongside the real inequality, justifying each real-valued entropy in the formula.
steps.lean: particle_kl_bound_of_finite_kl derives hn from positive particle count and proves hL by excluding zero smoothness: that case contradicts the admissible positive step. hs and hscaled express the lifted step restriction. ULA.LSI.ula_kl_bound supplies hfinite and hb for the actual summed potential. potential_differentiable and potential_gradient_lipschitz supply its analytic hypotheses; the remaining simplification uses finrank_state, lifted_entropy_rate_eq and lifted_entropy_bias_eq. No regular-interpolation data is an additional premise here.

steps.title: The entropy bound divided by particle count
steps.body:
Divide the finite joint entropy inequality by positive \(N\). Division preserves order and gives

\[\frac{H_k}{N}\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}\frac{H_0}{N}+\frac{8\gamma D L^2}{\beta}.\]

Because \(N>0\), every term is divided by the same finite positive number. The exponential is unchanged, and its initial factor is the initial joint entropy per particle. This is a numerical normalization of the joint divergence, not the divergence of the parameter marginal.
steps.lean:
particle_kl_bound_normalized_of_finite_kl obtains the finite joint divergence hfinite and full bound hb from particle_kl_bound_of_finite_kl. It keeps the former as the first component of its conclusion and applies normalize_entropy_bound to the latter. Thus every term of the full inequality, including the initial entropy, is divided by the same positive particle count.

The helper normalize_entropy_bound divides both the initial contribution and the bias, canceling one particle factor in the latter. The same finite-KL witness is retained for the unnormalized divergence. This quantity is the entropy of the full state divided by particle number; parameter projection is handled separately.

steps.title: A linearly scaled lifted logarithmic Sobolev constant
steps.body:
Assume the lifted Gibbs target has logarithmic Sobolev constant \(\beta=N\alpha\) with \(\alpha>0\). Positivity of particle count gives \(\beta>0\), and the restriction \(\gamma\le\beta/(4NL^2)\) becomes \(\gamma\le\alpha/(4L^2)\). Apply the normalized joint theorem with this constant. Its rate is \(e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\). The dimension equality \(D/N=d_x+d_\theta/N\) gives error term \((8\gamma L^2/\alpha)(d_x+d_\theta/N)\), so

\[\frac{H_k}{N}\le e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\frac{H_0}{N}+\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha}\left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right).\]

The functional-inequality premise concerns \(\Pi_N\) itself. The relation \(D/N=d_x+d_\theta/N\) separates the intensive latent and parameter contributions. Since the particles share a parameter, no product tensorization of independent pair targets is used to obtain the assumed constant.
steps.lean: particle_kl_bound_linear_lsi_of_finite_kl proves positive smoothness using ULA.LSI.positive_smoothness_of_step, then rewrites the step assumption with linear_lsi_step_iff. It applies the normalized theorem at the supplied linearly scaled lifted-target constant. The final rewrites linear_entropy_rate_eq and linear_normalized_entropy_bias_eq give the stated exponent and effective dimension while retaining finite joint divergence.

steps.title: The parameter-entropy consequence
steps.body:
Project both the particle law and its Gibbs reference to their parameter coordinates. Data processing gives \(\operatorname{KL}(\mu_k^\theta\Vert\Pi_N^\theta)\le H_k\). The joint theorem supplies \(H_k<\infty\), so the projected divergence is finite as well. Substitution of the full numerical estimate yields

\[\operatorname{KL}(\mu_k^\theta\Vert\Pi_N^\theta)\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}.\]

The initial quantity is the full joint entropy \(H_0\). The parameter divergence is unnormalized, so its error retains factor \(N\). If a joint bound is supplied per particle, it must first be multiplied by \(N\). Data processing changes only the left-hand divergence and does not replace the initial joint entropy by a smaller projected quantity.

It is the unnormalized joint estimate that is passed to data processing.
